<GlitchTitle>Technical Context</GlitchTitle>

:::note Note on incident chronology
Throughout this chapter, reference is made to the five phases through which the National Security Council's Analysis Committee structured the incident: **Phase 0** (pre-incident days and morning of 28 April, latent voltage instability); **Phase 1** (12:00–12:30 CEST, electromechanical oscillations preceding the root trip); **Phase 2** (12:32:00–12:33:18 CEST, first generation losses from overvoltage); **Phase 3** (12:33:18–12:33:30 CEST, disconnection cascade to voltage collapse); **Phase 4** (from 12:33:30 CEST, progressive supply restoration). Detailed chronology is presented in Chapters 4 and 5.
:::

## Generation fleet evolution: from synchronous machines to IBR-dominated mix

Despite more than a decade of structural stagnation in peak electricity demand in Spain, the generation fleet has undergone a profound transformation. Whereas in 2010 thermal and nuclear sources accounted for **65% of production**, by 2024 renewables had reversed that ratio, reaching **59% of the total mix**.

![Evolution of the generation mix in Spain (2010 vs. 2024)](/figuras/mix_comparativo_2010_2024.png) _Figure 4. Generation mix evolution in Spain: 2010 vs. 2024. Source: Peter Huber Centre / ESIOS._

By the first quarter of 2025, the peninsular system had consolidated this scenario, surpassing **100 GW of installed renewable capacity**. As of January 2025, almost 66% of total capacity came from decarbonised sources, with wind and solar PV in technical parity (24.9% each). Including distributed self-consumption, the global PV share exceeded **48.1 GW**, against **33.1 GW** of wind.

![Breakdown of installed generation capacity as of January 2025](/figuras/capacidad_instalada_2025.png) _Figure 5. Installed generation capacity in the Spanish system as of 31 January 2025. Source: NREL / Red Eléctrica._

As a direct counterpart, conventional synchronous generation has been progressively displaced: coal plays a residual role (**1.6%** of installed capacity), nuclear (**5.5%**) faces a progressive closure schedule, and more than **26 GW of combined-cycle gas turbines** (**20.4%**) operate at annual utilisation rates below 15%.

From a power systems engineering perspective, this transformation poses structural operational challenges. Historical network stability depended on synchronous generators — thermal, nuclear and hydraulic units — whose rotating masses provided immediate kinetic energy, <GlossaryLink term="Inercia (H)">physical inertia</GlossaryLink> and high fault currents. New solar and wind installations connect via <GlossaryLink term="IBR">inverters (_IBR_</GlossaryLink>), which operate in standard <GlossaryLink term="GFL (Grid-Following)">grid-following</GlossaryLink> mode: they synchronise their output to external voltage and frequency through <GlossaryLink term="Phase-Locked Loop (PLL)">PLL</GlossaryLink> algorithms and, lacking rotating masses, contribute neither synchronous inertia nor an intrinsic response to network fluctuations. The result is that the Iberian system routinely operates under conditions of low short-circuit capacity, high nodal impedance and amplified <GlossaryLink term="Tasa de Cambio de Frecuencia (RoCoF)">RoCoF</GlossaryLink> under any <GlossaryLink term="Potencia activa">active power</GlossaryLink> imbalance.

## Decarbonisation and operational implications

The environmental success of the Iberian energy transition is unambiguous. Sector emissions peaked at approximately **110 MtCO₂-eq** in 2007; by end- 2024, coinciding with a record renewable generation share (**56.8%**), they had fallen to **27.0 million tonnes of CO₂-eq** — a reduction of **75.7%** from the peak. The emission factor dropped from around 290 gCO₂/kWh in 2015 to approximately 80–100 gCO₂/kWh in 2024.

The operational counterpart is what this investigation examines: the substitution of thermal plants by inverter-connected renewable sources progressively withdraws the synchronous masses that provided inertia, dynamic <GlossaryLink term="Potencia reactiva">reactive power</GlossaryLink> and voltage control. The accelerated transition has led the Iberian system to routinely operate under low-inertia, low-nodal-strength conditions — whose relationship with the voltage instability of 28 April is analysed in Chapter 4.

## Pre-incident operational state: the abundance paradox

In the days preceding the blackout, the peninsular system operated under what technical literature has termed the **"abundance paradox"**. Unusually mild spring temperatures (~25 °C) and public holidays in several regions depressed the demand curve: at 12:30 CEST, minutes before the collapse, instantaneous demand stood at **25,184 MW** — **56%** of the system's historical peak demand.

This valley-demand scenario coincided with exceptional renewable resource availability, with non-synchronous generation covering **82% of the instantaneous mix**: approximately **18,000 MW** of solar PV (**53%**) and **3,500 MW** of wind (**11%**). To balance the active power surplus, the system simultaneously relied on hydraulic pumping (~3,000 MW) and net exports to France, Portugal and Morocco. Conventional synchronous generation was pushed to historical lows: nuclear at **10%** (3.4 GW) and gas combined cycles at a bare **3%** (~1,600 MW).

![Generation profile of the peninsular system on 28 April 2025](/figuras/ree_generation_mix_28april.png) _Figure 7. 28 April generation profile: valley demand coincided with the solar PV peak, displacing synchronous generation to historical lows. Source: NREL / Red Eléctrica._

This reduction in rotating masses translated into exceptionally low synchronous inertia values: **1.3 s** in the Southern area and **1.84 s** in the Central area — both below the 2 s threshold recommended by <GlossaryLink term="ENTSO-E">ENTSO-E</GlossaryLink>. Sustained operation under these conditions had already produced dynamic stress signals on **16, 22 and 24 April**, with voltage instability episodes on the transmission network.

![Voltage oscillations at Núñez de Balboa substation, 22 April 2025](/figuras/precursor_overvoltage_22april.png) _Figure 8. Voltage oscillations recorded at Núñez de Balboa (400 kV) during the precursor event of 22 April. Several plants that tripped on 28 April had already experienced identical trips during this prior event. Source: IIT-ICAI / Compass Lexecon._

The most severe precursor occurred on **22 April at ~19:00 h**: an overvoltage spike exceeding **430 kV** triggered protection relays, disconnecting multiple PV and wind plants. The fact that several installations which tripped in the first seconds of 28 April had already experienced identical trips in this prior event is interpreted by the ICAI report as evidence that the system was operating with **structurally narrow dynamic voltage control margins**.

## Interconnection capacity: the Iberian energy island

### The structural island condition

The Iberian Peninsula operates as an **«energy island»** within the Continental European synchronous area. Its exchange capacity with France historically sits between **3% and 5%** of installed generation capacity — or **7.9%** relative to peak demand — well below the EU's binding **15% target for 2030**. This constraint conditions supply security in two ways: perturbations originating in the European inertia centre are amplified as they propagate to the Iberian periphery (**whip effect**), and in the event of a massive generation loss, the interconnection bottleneck physically limits the dynamic support importable from large central European alternators.

### Commercial NTC versus physical power flows

A critical distinction must be drawn between commercial limits and actual physical flows. Market exchanges are governed by the Net Transfer Capacity (NTC), agreed _ex ante_ between <GlossaryLink term="REE">REE</GlossaryLink> and RTE. However, in fast transient conditions, active and reactive power flows obey Kirchhoff's laws regardless of market schedules. Forcing a physical flow beyond the angular stability limit — typically a 90° angular difference between terminals — does not increase transferred power but instead causes pole slip and consequent loss of <GlossaryLink term="Sincronismo">synchronism</GlossaryLink>: the mechanism that materialised on 28 April at **12:33:21 CEST**.

![Deviation between commercial NTC schedule and physical flow at the ES-FR border](/figuras/entsoe_flow_deviation.png) _Figure 9. Deviation between the commercial exchange programme (NTC) and the actual physical power flow at the Spain–France border during the morning of 28 April. Source: ENTSO-E Factual Report._

### The HVDC INELFE-1 link and the critical control mode decision

The French interconnection combines AC overhead lines with the underground <GlossaryLink term="HVDC">HVDC VSC</GlossaryLink> INELFE-1 link (Santa Llogaia–Baixas, **2,000 MW** nominal). This link supports three operationally relevant modes: **PMODE1** (constant power, no dynamic grid response), **PMODE2** (power modulation by frequency deviation) and **PMODE3** (AC emulation, responds to angular difference between terminals).

During the pre-incident period, INELFE-1 was operating in **PMODE3**. However, at **12:08 CEST**, to damp the 0.6 Hz oscillations detected in the system, the mode was switched to **PMODE1**, fixing an export of **1,000 MW** towards France. The consequences were critical: at the moment of collapse, AC transpyrenean lines attempted to import up to **4,609 MW** of emergency power from France, while the HVDC link — locked in PMODE1 — continued extracting 1,000 MW from the Iberian system, lacking an active frequency control loop that could reverse the flow direction. Effective support from the French system was thereby reduced relative to the theoretical maximum available. At **12:33:21 CEST**, the AC lines tripped on loss of synchronism, fully isolating the peninsula from the continental synchronous system.

![Control mode transition in the HVDC INELFE-1 link](/figuras/hvdc_control_transition.png) _Figure 10. PMODE3 → PMODE1 transition at 12:08 CEST in the HVDC INELFE-1 link. The decision limited the link's dynamic response capability during the subsequent cascade. Source: IIT-ICAI / AELEC._

### Southern border: Morocco and black start capability

The Moroccan connection (submarine AC cables, **900 MW** technical capacity) was supplying **314 MW** of imports moments before the collapse. At **12:33:20 CEST**, the Moroccan operator's underfrequency relays tripped at the **49.5 Hz** threshold, disconnecting the link to protect its network from Iberian instability propagation. While protective for Morocco, this disconnection had important implications for restoration: voltage injection from the south provided the reference needed hours later to initiate <GlossaryLink term="Black Start">Black Start</GlossaryLink> procedures for Andalusian combined-cycle plants.

## The European awareness system (EAS) and the «false normality»

### Operational state classification (SO GL)

The <GlossaryLink term="SO GL (System Operation Guidelines)">System Operation Guidelines</GlossaryLink> establish five progressive severity levels: **Normal** (compliance with the <GlossaryLink term="Criterio N-1">*N*−1 Criterion</GlossaryLink>), **Alert** (degraded security margins requiring preventive action), **Emergency** (security limit violations or <GlossaryLink term="UFLS (Underfrequency Load Shedding)">UFLS</GlossaryLink> activation), **Blackout** and **Restoration**.

### The abrupt Normal → Blackout transition

Analysis of <GlossaryLink term="EAS (ENTSO-E Awareness System)">EAS</GlossaryLink> records reveals a critical dissonance between the actual dynamics of the Iberian network and its representation on the European platform. During the morning of 28 April, the system experienced at least two significant oscillations: a forced oscillation at **0.6 Hz** at **12:03 CEST** and an inter-area mode at **0.2 Hz** at **12:19 CEST**. Despite this, neither REE nor REN declared an Alert state. At **12:32:00 CEST**, the official status remained «Normal». Records confirm that the system transitioned abruptly from **Normal** to **Blackout** (criterion OB3) at **12:33:29 CEST**, without passing through any intermediate phase.

This failure to escalate generated limited visibility for neighbouring operators. The French operator (RTE) received no signals of dynamic vulnerability south of the Pyrenees; with the EAS remaining at «Normal», no cross-border cooperation protocols were activated and the French network was not prepared for the transient that reached the border at 12:33:21 CEST. The episode demonstrates that the EAS acted not as an early warning tool but as a **post-mortem notifier** of the collapse — a structural limitation of the European monitoring system's ability to capture fast voltage dynamics in low-inertia networks, and one of the central regulatory lessons of the incident.

![Frequency and voltage evolution at Carmona substation (400 kV)](/figuras/frequency_voltage_carmona.png) _Figure 11. Frequency and voltage in the critical seconds of the incident. Carmona substation (400 kV). The abrupt Normal → Blackout transition is captured in the simultaneous collapse of both variables. Source: ENTSO-E / REE._

<GlitchTitle>Incident Analysis</GlitchTitle>

The voltage collapse of 28 April was not an instantaneous event: it was the culmination of a progressive, measurable degradation of the network's static and dynamic stability. The forensic reconstruction of the four collapse phases — from the morning oscillations to the definitive isolation of the peninsula at 12:33:29 CEST — allows precise identification of the physical mechanisms that no conventional protection automation could arrest.

## Phase 0: the weakened network and the meshing manoeuvre

On the morning of 28 April, the system was operating on an extremely weak topology. With demand at minimum levels, **35.8% of the 400 kV network in the southern zone** and **34.3% in the central zone** remained disconnected, creating a high transfer impedance scenario. Against this background, system dynamics manifested as <GlossaryLink term="Oscilaciones electromecánicas">electromechanical oscillations</GlossaryLink> in two distinct modes:

- **12:03 CEST** — Forced oscillation at **0.6 Hz**, amplitude 70 mHz, taking 4 minutes and 42 seconds to damp out.
- **12:19 CEST** — Inter-area mode at **0.2 Hz** (East-Centre-West): the Iberian Peninsula began oscillating in counter-phase with respect to the continent, stressing the Pyrenean interconnection links.

During both transients, the <GlossaryLink term="Damping ratio">damping ratio</GlossaryLink> collapsed to values near **1%**, well below the minimum **5%** threshold required by P.O. 13.1. This behaviour was not unprecedented: analogous episodes on 16, 22 and 24 April had been treated as isolated incidents rather than symptoms of systemic degradation.

![Voltages recorded at Núñez de Balboa 400 kV during precursor events and 28 April](/figuras/nunez_balboa_precursores.png) _Figure 12. Voltages at Núñez de Balboa (400 kV) during the 22, 24 and 28 April precursor events. The succession of overvoltage peaks evidences the progressive narrowing of <GlossaryLink term="Potencia reactiva">reactive power</GlossaryLink> control margins. Source: IIT-ICAI._

To contain these oscillations, REE executed a <GlossaryLink term="Mallado">meshing</GlossaryLink> manoeuvre: between 12:03 and 12:30 CEST it reconnected **11 400 kV lines** that had been open due to low demand. The manoeuvre achieved its immediate objective — reducing impedance and arresting the oscillation whip — but introduced, according to the IIT-ICAI expert report, a significant side effect: through the <GlossaryLink term="Efecto Ferranti">Ferranti Effect</GlossaryLink>, the no-load reconnected lines abruptly injected capacitive reactive power into a network that already lacked absorption margin. Quantification of this injection is one of the central axes of the technical dispute: the ICAI report estimates up to **2.4 GVAr**; the NREL's independent analysis adopts a more conservative estimate of **1,050 MVAr**. Both figures agree that the injection exceeded the system's residual absorption capacity, estimated at that moment at barely **3.3 GVAr** against the usual 5.8 GVAr.

IIT-ICAI's expert simulations estimate that after the meshing manoeuvre, the distance to the collapse point at the Carmona 400 kV bus contracted from **2,964 MW** to **1,268 MW** — a **57% reduction** bringing the system to the threshold of capacitive saturation.

![WAMS recording of the 0.6 Hz oscillation at 12:03 CEST in Carmona](/figuras/wams_oscilaciones_carmona.png) _Figure 13. <GlossaryLink term="WAMS (Wide Area Monitoring Systems)">WAMS</GlossaryLink> recording capturing the 0.6 Hz electromechanical oscillation at Carmona (Seville) at 12:03 CEST. WAMS systems, based on GPS-synchronised <GlossaryLink term="PMU (Phasor Measurement Unit)">PMU</GlossaryLink> networks, enable continental-scale dynamics to be observed with millisecond resolution. Source: ENTSO-E / REE._

## Phase 1: loss of damping and root trip (12:32:57 CEST)

The nature of the first transient — the 0.6 Hz oscillation at 12:03 CEST — is the subject of direct technical controversy. REE classifies it as a forced oscillation originating in the control loop of a photovoltaic plant in Badajoz. The ICAI report argues, conversely, that it was a natural inter-area mode exacerbated by a systemic damping ratio of **1%**, which it links to the absence of Power System Stabilisers (PSS) in the Andalusian combined-cycle units that were offline.

<BrowserOnly>
  {() => <FrequencyChart />}
</BrowserOnly>

![System frequency evolution during Phase 1 — NREL analysis](/figuras/timeline_frecuencia_nrel.png) _Figure 14. Frequency evolution during Phase 1. The two electromechanical oscillations and the progressive loss of system damping preceding the collapse are clearly visible. Source: NREL._

The instability intensified at **12:19 CEST** with the **0.2 Hz** mode, confirmed by European PMU telemetry as the natural East-Centre-West mode of the continental synchronous area: the Iberian Peninsula's reduced rotating mass was oscillating in counter-phase with the European inertia centre, materialising the whip effect described in Chapter 2.

The point of no return was reached at **12:32:57 CEST**. A 400/220 kV transformer at a collector substation in the province of **Granada** disconnected through overvoltage protection activation, having detected approximately **244 kV** on the 220 kV secondary — exceeding the equipment's dielectric safety threshold. The critical impact was not the 355 MW of <GlossaryLink term="Potencia activa">active power</GlossaryLink> lost — a manageable figure — but the instantaneous, irrecoverable loss of **165 MVAr** of inductive reactive power absorption capacity. In a system saturated with capacitive reactive power and operating with reduced <GlossaryLink term="Colapso Q-V">Q-V</GlossaryLink> margins, the disappearance of this sink caused a step increase in voltage at surrounding transmission nodes: the physical trigger of the chain reaction.

## Phase 2: the Tap-Lag phenomenon and voltage decoupling (12:32:57–12:33:18 CEST)

The 21 seconds following the root trip constitute the technical core of the forensic debate. After the Granada disconnection, the rising voltage trend on the transmission network revealed a divergence between the behaviour of the 400 kV infrastructure and the underlying collector networks: the <GlossaryLink term="Tap-Lag">Tap-Lag</GlossaryLink> phenomenon.

During Phase 1, voltage fluctuations caused by frequency oscillations had led 400/220 kV and 400/132 kV transformers to adjust their <GlossaryLink term="OLTC (On-Load Tap Changer)">OLTCs</GlossaryLink>, raising tap positions to boost secondary voltages. When the overvoltage surge hit the 400 kV network, these transformers were trapped by their own mechanical inertia: OLTC motor and gear mechanisms are intentionally slowed by time delays to prevent mechanical hunting under transient disturbances. Faced with an ultra-fast electrical transient, the tap changers proved too slow to reverse their transformation ratios in time.

![Oscillographic evidence of Tap-Lag voltage decoupling between 400 kV primary and collector secondary](/figuras/tap_lag_decoupling.png) _Figure 15. Voltage decoupling between the 400 kV primary and the collector secondary during Phase 2. While the voltage increase on the 400 kV side remained moderate, the OLTC inertia amplified the transient on the collector side. Source: ENTSO-E._

This mechanical failure created an **observability blindspot in REE's control room**. The <GlossaryLink term="SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition)">SCADA</GlossaryLink> system monitored the 400 kV primary, showing high but apparently compliant voltages below the exceptional normative limit of **435 kV** (P.O. 1.1). However, downstream, in the 220 kV and 132 kV networks, voltages climbed above **1.2 p.u.** — thresholds invisible to the national dispatch centre due to its limited observability of the underlying network.

![Overvoltage propagation heatmap across the transmission network during Phase 2](/figuras/heatmap_propagation.png) _Figure 16. Propagation of overvoltages across the 400 kV network during Phase 2 (12:32:00–12:33:18 CEST). Source: Government Analysis Committee / REE._

Faced with voltages exceeding their power electronics tolerances, solar and wind plant inverters triggered their internal overvoltage protection systems (ANSI function 59). This is where one of the incident's most consequential forensic disagreements arises: REE classified these losses as **«inadequate trips»**, arguing that no disconnection thresholds were exceeded on its 400 kV network; the ICAI analysis contends that the plants **acted correctly and in conformity with regulations** given the actual voltages experienced at their connection points, downstream of the OLTC transformers. The Tap-Lag phenomenon thereby created the conditions for a positive-feedback disconnection cascade.

## Phase 3: The Path to Voltage Zero (12:33:18—12:33:29 CEST)

<BrowserOnly>
  {() => <AnimatedMap lang="en" />}
</BrowserOnly>



In 11 seconds, the peninsular grid destroyed itself through a vicious cycle dictated by power flow equations. As IBR plants mass-disconnected to self-protect, the network instantly lost its capacity to absorb reactive power. Simultaneously, the falling active power reduced flow in the 400 kV lines, increasing their capacitive injection through the Ferranti Effect and driving voltages above **443 kV** at the most stressed nodes. Every disconnection raised voltage, forcing further disconnections.

![Spatial propagation of the generation loss cascade during Phase 3](/figuras/cascada_desconexiones.png) _Figure 17. Geographic propagation of the cascade during the eleven seconds of Phase 3. Source: Government Analysis Committee._

<span id="t6"></span>
The most severe losses were concentrated initially in **Badajoz** (at 12:33:16 CEST, *t=19 s*) and, in the immediately following second, at the **Segovia, Seville and Huelva** substations. In the five-second critical window (12:33:19–12:33:24 CEST), the chain reaction disconnected an order of magnitude close to **60% of the instantaneous national demand** in lost generation, taking the system beyond any possibility of recovery. (For the exhaustive second-by-second chronology and the exact power volumes of each disconnection, see [**Table 16 / Timeline**](./16-galeria-forense.mdx) in the Forensic Gallery).

<BrowserOnly>
  {() => <EnergyMixChart />}
</BrowserOnly>

As the cascade destroyed remaining generation, frequency collapsed with extreme <GlossaryLink term="RoCoF (Rate of Change of Frequency)">RoCoF</GlossaryLink>, activating <GlossaryLink term="UFLS (Underfrequency Load Shedding)">UFLS</GlossaryLink> schemes. At the **49.5 Hz** threshold crossing at 12:33:20 CEST, over **2,000 MW** of hydraulic pumping was automatically shed, followed by multiple industrial demand steps.

![Coupled evolution of voltage and frequency during Phase 3](/figuras/tension_frecuencia_colapso.png) _Figure 18. Coupled evolution of voltage (kV) and frequency (Hz) during Phase 3. The voltage increase above 1.10 p.u. precedes the frequency collapse in time, confirming the incident as a primarily capacitive, not inertial, collapse. Source: Government Analysis Committee._

The UFLS activation revealed what analysts have termed the **UFLS paradox**: by shedding active load to stabilise frequency, the scheme simultaneously eliminated the inductive reactive power consumption of that same demand. In a network saturated with capacitive reactive power, removing the last inductive sinks — the disconnected motors and industrial loads — produced a renewed overvoltage surge, **reinforcing the very collapse the UFLS was designed to arrest**. Protection logic designed for frequency deficit events proved counterproductive against a collapse driven primarily by voltage instability.

<span id="t2"></span>
In the final moments, the massive internal generation deficit triggered a violent reversal of Pyrenean flows: the AC lines attempted to import an emergency reactive magnitude exceeding **4,500 MVAr** from France. Simultaneously, HVDC link INELFE-1 — locked in PMODE1 since 12:08 CEST — continued extracting active power on the order of **1 GW** from the Iberian system (the precise breakdown by circuit and capacity can be audited in [**Table 14**](./15-galeria-de-tablas.mdx) and in the **Forensic Charts 1-5**, Interconnections category). This asymmetric operation drastically reduced the net support capacity from the continent.

![France interconnection exchange and loss of synchronism during Phase 3](/figuras/interconexion_francia_colapso.png) _Figure 19. Pyrenean flow reversal during Phase 3: emergency import of up to 4,609 MW via AC lines, simultaneous 1,000 MW HVDC extraction in PMODE1, and AC line trip on loss of synchronism at 12:33:21 CEST. Source: Government Analysis Committee / REE._

At **12:33:21 CEST**, loss-of- <GlossaryLink term="Sincronismo">synchronism</GlossaryLink> protections opened the AC interconnection links to prevent propagation to the continental European system, fully isolating the Iberian Peninsula. The definitive **voltage zero** was confirmed at **12:33:29.741 CEST** with the trip of the last generating unit — closing the most severe systemic incident documented in the history of the continental European power system.

<GlitchTitle>Response & Restoration</GlitchTitle>

Following the voltage zero at 12:33:30 CEST, the peninsular power system transitioned from an uncontrollable dynamic crisis to a phase of emergency management and structural restoration. The loss of over 15 GW and total disconnection from the continental synchronous system forced REE to abandon steady-state operating logic and activate the emergency protocols of **Operating Procedure P.O. 1.6**. Full supply restoration required nearly **19 hours** of uninterrupted manoeuvring.

## Collapse and restoration timeline

<ForensicTable 
    title="TABLA 2 | INCIDENT CHRONOLOGY — RECOVERY PHASES"
    source="Comité de Análisis del Gobierno"
    confidence="HIGH"
  >

| Phase | Time window | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Phase 0** | Pre-incident days and morning of 28 April | Latent voltage instability |
| **Phase 1** | 12:00–12:30 CEST | Electromechanical oscillations |
| **Phase 2** | 12:32:00–12:33:18 CEST | Generation losses from overvoltage |
| **Phase 3** | 12:33:18–12:33:30 CEST | Disconnection cascade to voltage zero |
| **Phase 4** | 12:33:30 CEST – 14:36 on 29 April | Progressive supply restoration |



</ForensicTable>

_Official phase chronology per the Government Analysis Committee._

## Emergency management: P.O. 1.1 and P.O. 1.6 activation

P.O. 1.1 establishes steady-state operating criteria, grounded in <GlossaryLink term="Criterio N-1">*N*−1 Criterion</GlossaryLink> compliance and the maintenance of transmission voltages between 380 kV and 435 kV. The 28 April cascade exposed the limitations of static security validation against ultra-fast dynamic transients in low- <GlossaryLink term="Inercia (H)">inertia</GlossaryLink> networks: security limits were breached within an eleven-second window, and automatic defence schemes — including <GlossaryLink term="UFLS (Underfrequency Load Shedding)">UFLS</GlossaryLink> — proved counterproductive. REE assumed manual control under _Blackout_ state (criterion OB3).

The institutional response was immediate and simultaneous across several fronts:

- **12:34 CEST** — REE confirms with REN that the entire Portuguese network is likewise de-energised.
- **12:36 CEST** — Formal notification to all European TSOs via the <GlossaryLink term="EAS (ENTSO-E Awareness System)">EAS</GlossaryLink>,
  updating the Iberian bloc's operational status to «Restoration».
- **12:44 CEST** — REE and OMIE suspend all intraday markets and balancing services, granting full authority to dispatch generators exclusively on technical and thermodynamic viability criteria.

The recovery strategy prescribed the controlled fragmentation of the Iberian Peninsula into **seven independent operating areas** — Southern Zone, Tajo-Centre, Levante and others — during progressive re-energisation.

![Topological fragmentation of the peninsula into seven electrical islands during restoration](/figuras/islas_reposicion_entsoe.png) _Figure 20. Topological fragmentation under P.O. 1.6. Each island had to individually stabilise its voltage and frequency parameters before synchronisation with adjacent islands was authorised. Source: ENTSO-E / REE._

The manoeuvre combined two simultaneous fronts: a **Top-Down** strategy (external support from France and Morocco as stable voltage reference) and a **Bottom-Up** strategy (autonomous start-up of internal hydroelectric plants in Galicia, Asturias and the Duero basin).

## Black Start strategy: hydroelectric plants and combined cycles

With virtually the entire generation fleet composed of <GlossaryLink term="IBR">IBR</GlossaryLink> operating in <GlossaryLink term="GFL (Grid-Following)">grid-following</GlossaryLink> mode — technologically incapable of generating a voltage waveform without a stable external grid reference — the survival and restart of the system fell exclusively on synchronous machines equipped with <GlossaryLink term="Black Start">autonomous start-up</GlossaryLink> capability.

![Dual re-energisation strategy: Top-Down and Bottom-Up](/figuras/estrategia_reenergizacion_dual.png) _Figure 21. Dual re-energisation strategy: Top-Down via France and Morocco; Bottom-Up via internal hydroelectric plants. Source: ENTSO-E / REE._

Hydroelectric plants — run-of-river and pumped storage — were the first units dispatched to energise isolated network sections and form the initial electrical islands. However, operating these micro-systems revealed the difficulty of functioning with minimal inertia: no-load line energisation triggered significant capacitive transients that prevented the completion of multiple start-up attempts.

![Temporal deployment and effectiveness of hydroelectric Black Start attempts](/figuras/black_start_hidroelectrico.png) _Figure 22. Hydroelectric Black Start attempts during Phase 4. Grey dots represent failed attempts. The high proportion of failures reflects the complexity of energising a network without coupled synchronous mass. Source: ENTSO-E / REE._

The failures were significant: the Cantabria and Levante islands collapsed and had to be restarted; the unit assigned to Madrid failed to stabilise its parameters after several consecutive attempts; and autonomous start-up in Andalusia proved unsuccessful, requiring external support from Morocco as the voltage reference for the southern zone.

Once the hydroelectric islands achieved minimum parameter stabilisation, the strategy shifted towards electromechanical consolidation through Gas Combined-Cycle Turbines (CCGT) and nuclear auxiliary services. These units were not connected to supply commercial demand, but to form the system's **«electromagnetic scaffolding»**: they provided the short-circuit power ($S_{sc}$), inertia ($H$) and dynamic <GlossaryLink term="Potencia reactiva">reactive power</GlossaryLink> management capacity indispensable before authorising mass load reconnection.

The Portuguese system executed an analogous scheme based on HPP 1-Centro and CCGT 1-Norte. At **20:22 CEST**, the synchronisation of Portuguese islands with Spanish zones already coupled to the continental European frequency — verified via _synchro-check_ relays — guaranteed the viability of full Iberian Peninsula restoration.

## International coordination: RCC, Swissgrid and continental resynchronisation

The tools of the Regional Coordination Centres (RCC) — in particular Coreso, responsible for Southwest Europe — evaluate security through static power flow calculations in steady-state conditions, without capability to anticipate <GlossaryLink term="Estabilidad de tensión">voltage instability</GlossaryLink> phenomena or ultra-fast dynamics associated with low inertia. Consequently, all pre-collapse analyses returned «OK» status, and the Iberian bloc remained labelled «Normal» in the EAS until the instant of the blackout.

Once the voltage zero was confirmed, the European command hierarchy activated through the Synchronous Area Monitors (SAM), operated by Swissgrid and Amprion. Between **12:49 and 12:54 CEST**, a unified command structure was established:

- **REE** → frequency leader for the disconnected Iberian island
- **Swissgrid** → stabilisation of the remainder of the continent
- **RTE (France)** → overall resynchronisation leader

Under this framework, RTE activated bids in its internal balancing mechanism for up to **4,500 MW** to sustain exports to Spain, enabling the energisation of the 400 kV corridors in the north and east of the peninsula.

![Evolution of cross-border support from France during restoration](/figuras/evolucion_carga_repuesta_francia.png) _Figure 23. Cross-border support from France during restoration. RTE injections sustained voltage stability during the re-energisation of northern and eastern corridors before sufficient internal synchronous units were coupled. Source: Government Analysis Committee._

On the southern border, the Morocco interconnection (ONEE) became the **electromechanical anchor for Andalusia**. At **13:04 CEST**, power flow was enabled via the Puerto de la Cruz–Mellousa line, injecting approximately **900 MW** and providing the voltage reference needed to energise the southern peninsula, where internal Black Start attempts had failed.

![Power injection from Morocco for Top-Down support in Andalusia](/figuras/intercambio_marruecos_topdown.png) _Figure 24. Top-Down support from the southern border (ONEE). The Moroccan interconnection proved decisive in providing the short-circuit power needed to energise Andalusia. Source: ENTSO-E / REE._

ENTSO-E's expert panel subsequently recognised this cooperation as a case of **effective coordination among European operators** under maximum severity events (OB3).

## Mix evolution and final stabilisation

Despite solar and wind farms being physically intact with primary resource available, their reconnection was restricted during the critical early phases. Grid-following inverters require a pre-existing robust external network to inject current through their <GlossaryLink term="Phase-Locked Loop (PLL)">PLL</GlossaryLink> loops: without that reference, they are inoperable. The full burden of re-energisation fell on the sequential coupling of CCGTs, remaining coal plants and nuclear auxiliary services.

![Evolution of the technology mix during peninsular re-energisation](/figuras/evolucion_mix_reenergizacion.png) _Figure 25. Technology mix during re-energisation. In the first critical hours, the system was sustained exclusively by cross-border imports and synchronous generation. IBR reconnection was restricted until minimum short-circuit power and inertia levels were accredited. Source: ENTSO-E / REE._

Load was reconnected in discrete, carefully calculated blocks:

- **13:07 CEST** — First **31 MW** supplied through Irún substation.
- **23:32 CEST** — With 21 thermal units synchronised, covered demand reached **13,039 MW** (~55% of expected load).
- **00:06 CEST (29 April)** — REE reactivated the automatic frequency restoration reserve (aFRR) master controller, restoring automated secondary regulation and load-frequency control.
- **01:38 CEST (29 April)** — First dispatch signals authorising active injection from wind farms and cogeneration plants.
- **07:05 CEST (29 April)** — Restrictions lifted for all RCR installations. REE certifies restoration of **99.95%** of national electricity supply.

![Demand collapse and recovery over the 19 hours following voltage zero](/figuras/recuperacion_demanda_peninsular.png) _Figure 26. Peninsular demand collapse and recovery. Restoration of the lost 25 GW was completed after nearly 19 hours of uninterrupted manoeuvring, with staged load reconnection to prevent further underfrequency events. Source: Government Analysis Committee._

The restoration sequence provides empirical confirmation of the central technical argument of this work: synchronous generation — absent in sufficient quantities during pre-collapse operation — proved to be the only electromechanical substrate capable of sustaining recovery. Its role as «scaffolding» for re-energisation is not an operational artefact, but a direct consequence of the fundamental physical properties that IBR in grid-following mode cannot replicate.

<GlitchTitle>Analysis of Official Reports</GlitchTitle>

The cross-analysis of the four reports on the 28 April blackout reveals an architecture of disputes that goes well beyond technical disagreement: three institutionally opposed narratives of the same sequence of events, with direct legal, economic and regulatory implications. This chapter examines the internal coherence of each narrative, their verified points of consensus, and their irreconcilable contradictions.

## The Government and REE position: multifactorial causality and regulatory non-compliance

The official narrative classifies the blackout not as an operational design error or a direct consequence of dispatch manoeuvres, but as a **multifactorial event**: the convergence of valley demand, massive <GlossaryLink term="IBR">IBR</GlossaryLink> penetration and inadequate technical behaviour by private agents that, acting simultaneously, exceeded the thresholds of the <GlossaryLink term="Criterio N-1">*N*−1 Security Criterion</GlossaryLink>.

<ForensicTable 
    title="TABLA 3 | MULTI-FACTOR CAUSALITY MODEL"
    source="Comité de Análisis del Gobierno / REE"
  >

| Factor | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **Insufficient voltage control** | Non-compliance with P.O. 7.4 by synchronous generators and RCR installations |
| **Electromechanical oscillations** | Conditioning factors for the pre-collapse system state |
| **Generation disconnections** | Some classified as premature → final vector of the overvoltage cascade |



</ForensicTable>

_Multifactorial causality scheme per the Government Analysis Committee._

REE's technical defence of the <GlossaryLink term="Mallado">meshing</GlossaryLink> manoeuvre merits careful examination. The report highlights an aspect frequently omitted from criticism: the initial oscillations produced not overvoltages but **voltage drops** at transmission network nodes. Against this risk, the Control Centre executed strictly protocolised actions — circuit reconnection, shunt reactor coupling, HVDC coordination to switch to PMODE1 — acknowledging that these manoeuvres «contributed to the voltage rise» but classifying them as necessary. REE argues that any subsequent voltage increase would have been absorbable had agents complied with their regulatory obligations.

![Thermal voltage maps of the 400 kV network in the moments preceding the root trip](/figuras/mapas_termicos_tension_ree.png) _Figure 27. Voltage mapping of the 400 kV network (12:30–12:32:57 CEST) per the System Operator's analysis. REE maintains that voltage profiles remained within P.O. 1.1 operating ranges until the onset of disconnections in the underlying collector networks. Source: Red Eléctrica._

The central argument transfers responsibility to the generation fleet: analysis of the 850 highest-generating installations documents that approximately **22%** did not meet the power factor criterion under RD 413/2014, though the report itself notes this may be partly attributable to the capacitive effect of evacuation infrastructure under low generation. A thermal plant in the southern zone not only failed to absorb inductive <GlossaryLink term="Potencia reactiva">reactive power</GlossaryLink>, but injected additional capacitive reactive power into the system. For REE, the collective inhibition of the private fleet deprived the system of the dynamic margin needed to contain the transient.

On inertia, REE explicitly rules it out as the material cause: the system operated with $H = 2.3$ s, above the 2 s threshold recommended by <GlossaryLink term="ENTSO-E">ENTSO-E</GlossaryLink>, and «the overvoltage wave would have triggered the cascade effect in any case», since overvoltage conditions persisted until 12:33:23 CEST independently of frequency.

The government narrative shows appreciable internal coherence and identifies documented regulatory breaches. However, it does not address two key arguments from the ICAI expert report: the magnitude of the capacitive reactive power injected by the meshing manoeuvre, and the operator's observability limitation on the 220 kV network through the <GlossaryLink term="Tap-Lag">Tap-Lag</GlossaryLink> phenomenon — two elements which, according to ICAI, would have made the collapse inevitable regardless of generator compliance levels.

### Official sequence of triggering events (REE)

<ForensicTable 
    title="TABLA 4 | OFFICIAL EVENT SEQUENCE LOG"
    source="Red Eléctrica (REE)"
  >

| No. | Ref. | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | N-1 | Forced oscillation at 0.6 Hz (possible origin: PV plant, Badajoz). Protocolised measures: reactors, line coupling, programme changes. |
| 2 | N-2 | Natural inter-area mode at 0.2 Hz. Further damping manoeuvres. |
| 3 | N-3 | P.O. 7.4 generation does not absorb required reactive power by setpoint. |
| 4 | N-4 | RCR generation variations affect voltage control. ~22% of plants fail power factor criterion. |
| 5 | — | Requested conventional generation after oscillations fails to couple. |
| 6 | N-5 | Distributed generation (&lt;1 MW) and self-consumption losses (435 MW) before 12:32:57. |
| 7 | **N-6** | **Root trip of evacuation transformer in Granada at 12:32:57.** REE records 418 kV at 400 kV — within normative limits. |
| 8 | N-7 | CSP and PV trips in Badajoz, no information at transmission network border. |
| 9 | N-8 | PV trip in Badajoz (different substation), no visibility at border. |
| 10–14 | — | Trips in Segovia, Huelva, Seville, Cáceres and Badajoz, no border information. |
| 15 | N-11 | Combined-cycle trip in Valencia. |
| 16 | — | UFLS triggers additional voltage rise through line discharge. |
| 17 | — | HVDC INELFE-1 continues exporting 1,000 MW in PMODE1. |
| 18 | N-12 | Nuclear unit trip. Loss of synchronism and voltage zero at **12:33:29.741 CEST**. |



</ForensicTable>

### Redeia's regulatory proposals

<ForensicTable 
    title="TABLA 5 | PROPOSED REGULATORY AMENDMENTS"
    source="Redeia / REE"
  >

| Area | Proposed measure |
| --- | --- |
| **Dynamic voltage control** | New P.O. 7.4: mandate real-time voltage control for all capable generation, with penalties for non-compliance. Revision of overvoltage thresholds. Deployment of <GlossaryLink term="Compensadores Síncronos (SynCons)">synchronous condensers</GlossaryLink> or <GlossaryLink term="Compensador Síncrono Estático (STATCOM)">STATCOMs</GlossaryLink>. |
| **Operation and stability** | Extension of generation programme change ramps to minimum 10 minutes. Update of pre-Orden TED/749/2020 RCR generation. Activation of power-frequency control on HVDC links. |
| **Observability** | Enhanced voltage control in distribution. System Operator access to self-consumption observability. Expansion of <GlossaryLink term="WAMS (Wide Area Monitoring Systems)">WAMS</GlossaryLink> with one <GlossaryLink term="PMU (Phasor Measurement Unit)">PMU</GlossaryLink> per transmission park. |
| **Monitoring** | Fault recording at minimum 20 ms sampling with time synchronisation. Centralised incident data collection platform. |



</ForensicTable>

## The generator sector position (ICAI / AELEC): excessive meshing and inevitable collapse

In contrast to the government narrative, the IIT-ICAI expert report — together with Compass Lexecon and INESC TEC — formally diagnoses the event as a **voltage collapse**: a <GlossaryLink term="Estabilidad de tensión">voltage instability</GlossaryLink> phenomenon driven by the exhaustion of reactive power absorption capacity, in which REE's own preventive actions acted as the primary cascade vector.

The core of the critique is quantitative. In response to oscillations from 12:03 CEST, REE coupled **11 no-load 400 kV circuits**. Through the <GlossaryLink term="Efecto Ferranti">Ferranti Effect</GlossaryLink>, these lines behaved as large capacitor banks, injecting between **1.05 and 2.4 GVAr** of capacitive reactive power into a network already lacking absorption margin. Simulations estimate that the collapse margin at the Carmona 400 kV bus contracted from **2,964 MW** to **1,268 MW** — a **57% reduction** bringing the system to the threshold of capacitive saturation.

![Q-V curves at Carmona 400 kV bus per ICAI expert analysis](/figuras/fluctuaciones_tension_previas.png) _Figure 28. <GlossaryLink term="Colapso Q-V">Q-V</GlossaryLink> voltage stability curves at Carmona 400 kV. The meshing manoeuvres (LIN&SHN) displaced the operating point, contracting the collapse margin by 57%. The red dashed line marks the V = 1.2 p.u. limit (480 kV). Source: IIT-ICAI / Compass Lexecon._

The discrepancy between ICAI's (2.4 GVAr) and NREL's independent (1.05 GVAr) estimates does not alter the shared conclusion: in both cases, the capacitive injection exceeded the system's residual absorption capacity, estimated at barely **3.3 GVAr** against the usual 5.8 GVAr.

On the cascade disconnections, the generator sector refutes the «inadequate trips» classification by pointing to the operator's observability limitation. While the <GlossaryLink term="SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition)">SCADA</GlossaryLink> showed 418 kV on the 400 kV network — within normative limits — the Tap-Lag phenomenon created a blind spot in the collector networks: the mechanical inertia of the <GlossaryLink term="OLTC (On-Load Tap Changer)">OLTCs</GlossaryLink> amplified the transient to the 220 kV networks, where **244 kV** (>110% nominal voltage) was reached. The owner of the Granada substation confirmed that its protection «was correctly set and operated correctly».

![Oscillographic record of the root trip in Granada at 12:32:56.993 CEST](/figuras/aluvion_alertas_sobretension_sur.png) _Figure 29. Oscillogram of the root trip (Granada, 12:32:56.993 CEST). Upper panel: three-phase current stable until upstream breaker trip. Lower panel: collector secondary voltage — phase A reaches ~145 kV (>1.10 p.u.) — invisible to REE's SCADA on the 400 kV network through the Tap-Lag effect. Source: IIT-ICAI / AELEC._

The second argument line targets the regulatory framework: P.O. 7.4, in its pre-reform version, forced IBR to operate at a **fixed power factor**, preventing their power electronics from dynamically absorbing or injecting reactive power despite possessing this technological capability. This restriction excluded **82% of instantaneous generation** from active voltage control, concentrating operational responsibility on the scarce available synchronous thermal fleet.

The resulting quantitative imbalance was, per the expert report, **mathematically insurmountable**: in the southern zone, REE had barely **0.2 GVAr** of inductive reactive absorption capacity against an estimated capacitive injection exceeding **0.7 GVAr** induced by its own manoeuvres.

![Reactive power balance in the southern zone at 12:30 CEST per IIT-ICAI](/figuras/asimetria_balance_reactiva_sur.png) _Figure 30. Reactive power balance at 12:30 CEST. REE's manoeuvres added 0.7 GVAr capacitive on top of the existing 3.4 GVAr, while conventional synchronous generation provided barely 0.2 GVAr of absorption. Net deficit: −0.6 GVAr. Source: IIT-ICAI / Compass Lexecon._

The expert report's conclusion identifies **three factors directly attributable to the operator and regulator**: the meshing manoeuvre that saturated Q-V margins, the structural inobservability of the 220 kV network through Tap-Lag, and the regulatory framework (P.O. 7.4) that prevented 82% of the generation fleet from participating in dynamic voltage control.

## The European perspective (ENTSO-E): NC RfG inadequacy and synchronous separation

ENTSO-E's expert panel offers the most structural of the three perspectives. Its central thesis rejects attribution of the blackout to renewable penetration _per se_: the collapse resulted not from excess renewable generation or primary inertia shortage, but from the **limitations of the voltage profile control framework**. The incident reveals the asymmetry between accelerated renewable asset deployment and the partial obsolescence of the network codes governing their dynamic behaviour.

The analysis identifies a fundamental technical tension: most of the installations that disconnected possessed the power electronics needed for robust voltage control, but Spanish regulations **prohibited or did not require** this dynamic service, forcing them to operate at static power factors under RD 413/2014. This regulatory restriction deprived the system of the distributed reactive support that could have damped the capacitive injection from no-load lines.

In direct response, ENTSO-E has consolidated in its Phase II Report the update to **NC RfG 2.0**, which proposes mandating <GlossaryLink term="GFM (Grid-Forming)">grid-forming</GlossaryLink> operation for all non-synchronous modules ≥ 1 MW:

<ForensicTable 
    title="TABLA 6 | NC RFG 2.0 (PROPOSED) REQUIREMENTS COMPARISON"
    source="ENTSO-E (Phase II Report)"
  >

| Requirement | <GlossaryLink term="NC RfG">Current NC RfG</GlossaryLink> | NC RfG 2.0 (proposed) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Operating mode | _Grid-following_ | _Grid-forming_ mandatory |
| Threshold | Varies by type/country | ≥ 1 MW (PPM and ESM) |
| Voltage control | Fixed power factor | Continuous dynamic V and Q control |
| Inertia | Not required for IBR | <GlossaryLink term="Inercia Sintética">Synthetic inertia</GlossaryLink> mandatory |
| Black Start | Not required for IBR | Island start-up capability |
| Synchronism reference | External (PLL on grid) | Internally generated (ideal voltage source) |



</ForensicTable>

On the topology of the incident, ENTSO-E analyses the loss of <GlossaryLink term="Sincronismo">synchronism</GlossaryLink> at **12:33:19 CEST**: the system passed from exporting 469 MW (12:32:57) to importing a maximum of **3,807 MW** (12:33:19), at which point the angular pole slip became unsustainable and _Out-of-Step_ (OST) protections acted at **12:33:21 CEST**, ordering the opening of the transpyrenean circuits.

![Spain-France exchange evolution and loss of synchronism (12:32:57–12:33:20 CEST)](/figuras/perdida_sincronismo_frontera.png) _Figure 31. Active power exchange at the Spain-France border during Phase 3. Upper panel: total net flow (469 MW export → 3,807 MW maximum import). Lower panel: per-circuit breakdown. The terminal oscillation reflects pole divergence prior to definitive breaker opening. Source: ENTSO-E._

This separation prevented the capacitive collapse and frequency collapse — with a <GlossaryLink term="RoCoF (Rate of Change of Frequency)">RoCoF</GlossaryLink> exceeding **1.5 Hz/s** — from propagating to the French system and the rest of Continental Europe.

ENTSO-E's final warning is structural: coordinated security analyses (CSA) and Common Grid Models (CGM), based on static load flows and the *N*−1 Criterion, **assessed the system as «Normal»** until moments before the collapse. For ENTSO-E, this limitation indicates that continental operative security assessment standards — designed for conventional synchronous machines — are structurally insufficient to prevent collapses in systems with high power electronics penetration.

## Consensus and divergences: the technical fracture across three axes

### Verified technical consensus

Despite the polarisation of the debate, the four reports converge on a set of technical conclusions that qualify or refute the most widespread media narratives:

<ForensicTable 
    title="TABLA 7 | TECHNICAL CONSENSUS MATRIX"
    source="Elaboración propia"
  >

| Consensus point | Shared technical basis | GOV | REE | ICAI | ENTSO-E |
| --- | --- | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: |
| **Inertia was not the root cause** | System operated at H = 2.3 s (above 2.0 s threshold). Greater inertia would have slowed the frequency collapse by fractions of a second, without preventing the overvoltage collapse. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **Overvoltage collapse, not frequency deficit** | The material cause was capacitive instability (reactive power Q imbalance), not active power P loss or primary frequency drop. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **Active power reserves were sufficient** | Upward tertiary reserve exceeded 7,000 MW. No generation capacity crisis occurred. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **UFLS aggravated the voltage collapse** | Load shedding eliminated the last inductive reactive sinks, accelerating the voltage escalation. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **Synchronism protections acted correctly** | The opening of transpyrenean circuits at 12:33:21 was technically and normatively correct. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **IBR regulatory framework was inadequate** | P.O. 7.4 and RD 413/2014 prevented IBR from participating in dynamic voltage control despite possessing the technological capability. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **Static N−1 criterion is insufficient** | Static security tools assessed the system as safe hours before the collapse, unable to anticipate ultra-fast capacitive instability dynamics. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |



</ForensicTable>

### Irreconcilable technical divergences

<ForensicTable 
    title="TABLA 8 | TECHNICAL DIVERGENCE MATRIX"
    source="Elaboración propia"
  >

| Dispute axis | Government / REE | ICAI / AELEC | ENTSO-E |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Origin of capacitive saturation** | The system had sufficient margins. Saturation occurred because generators failed to absorb required reactive power. The meshing manoeuvre was protocolised and necessary. | Meshing 11 no-load lines injected 1.05–2.4 GVAr capacitive via the Ferranti Effect, contracting the Q-V margin at Carmona by 57%. The collapse was mathematically inevitable. | Does not attribute causality to meshing but documents that RCCs did not detect the saturation. Identifies IBR regulatory restriction as the primary structural vulnerability. |
| **2. Nature of the 0.6 Hz oscillation** | Forced oscillation originating in the control loop of a PV plant in Badajoz: trigger of the sequence leading to collapse. | Evidence is inconclusive. Could be a natural inter-area mode amplified by the ~1% damping ratio, due to absence of active PSS in the offline southern CCGTs. | Documents the oscillation as atypical (detected as far as Germany) but assigns no definitive causality. |
| **3. Legitimacy of cascade trips (Tap-Lag)** | First trips (12:32:57–12:33:18) were «inadequate» or premature: SCADA recorded 418 kV on the 400 kV network, within P.O. 1.1 limits. | Trips were normatively correct. Tap-Lag created a blind spot: 220 kV collector networks reached 244 kV (>1.10 p.u.), invisible to SCADA. The Granada substation owner confirmed the protection operated correctly. | Does not classify trips as inadequate. Highlights network inobservability as a systemic limitation of both the operator and RCCs. |
| **4. Southern zone dispatch** | Acknowledges unavailability of the Andalusian CCGT from 27 April afternoon. Justifies non-substitution by adequate voltage levels at that time. | The southern zone had only 0.2 GVAr of absorption against >0.7 GVAr of capacitive injection induced by the operator itself. Non-substitution was the most determinative dispatch decision of the incident. | Identifies low short-circuit power in Andalusia as a structural aggravating factor, without commenting on the individual decision. |
| **5. Primary responsibility** | Generators breached their voltage control obligations. The blackout was a failure of the private generation fleet. | REE drove the network to an inevitable collapse state through meshing, with insufficient observability and inadequate dispatch. Generators acted per physics and regulation. The blackout was a failure of the operator and regulator. | The root cause is regulatory: the restriction preventing IBR from dynamically controlling voltage. The failure belongs to the European and national regulatory system, not attributable exclusively to any single agent. |



</ForensicTable>

## Interpretive synthesis: three governance fractures

The comparative analysis allows the inter-party dispute to be transcended in favour of a second-order diagnosis: the 28 April 2025 blackout was neither an unforeseeable «black swan» nor the failure of a specific technology, but the **convergent manifestation of three governance fractures** coexisting in the Iberian power system.

### Operational fracture: causality versus responsibility

The meshing-as-trigger thesis (ICAI) and the collective non-compliance thesis (REE / Government) are not mutually exclusive in technical terms: both factors contributed to the capacitive saturation that narrowed the Q-V margins. What they are mutually exclusive in is their legal and economic implication. This causal ambiguity is the predictable result of operating a network without sufficient dynamic instrumentation: when the system lacks PMU coverage at all critical nodes and real-time voltage stability calculation tools, subsequent forensic reconstruction is inevitably subject to interpretation. The tacit consensus among all parties — which no report states explicitly — is that the **monitoring architecture proved insufficient** both for managing the incident in real time and for resolving it unambiguously after the fact.

### Regulatory fracture: 20th-century regulation applied to a 21st-century grid

ENTSO-E's position — the most structural of the three — argues that both the operator and generators acted within the limits of a regulatory framework that was inadequate for the system it purported to govern. P.O. 7.4 and RD 413/2014 designed a voltage control scheme for a network dominated by slowly-responding synchronous masses; applying this to a grid with 82% IBR penetration is, in control engineering terms, equivalent to attempting to stabilise a millisecond-response system with a regulator designed for minute-scale dynamics. This inadequacy was not unknown: the P.O. 7.4 update proposal had been **pending regulatory approval for years**. The Government's own report acknowledges that its entry into force would have been the most relevant change to have prevented the collapse. The 28 April blackout is, in this sense, the **measurable cost of a regulatory delay**.

### Systemic fracture: static security tools in a dynamic network

The unanimous consensus on the insufficiency of the static *N*−1 Criterion points to a vulnerability that extends well beyond the Iberian case. The load flow models that evaluated the system as «Normal» are mathematically incapable of representing capacitive instability phenomena in low-inertia networks: they do not solve differential equations, do not model inverter control loop dynamics, and do not calculate Q-V margins in real time. The speed of collapse progression — from first trips to voltage zero in under **90 seconds** — places the phenomenon outside the temporal horizon of any human intervention: when the operator perceived the severity of the transient, the system was already irrecoverable. The only viable response at this timescale is **structural prevention through real-time dynamic security analysis**, whose deployment at European regional coordination centres constitutes one of the most urgent reforms identified by ENTSO-E.

### The limit of the centralised paradigm

Underlying the three fractures is a deeper tension that the reports address fragmentarily but which comparative analysis allows to be formulated clearly: the centralised operation paradigm — a single operator with visibility limited to the 400 kV level, managing voltage with discrete switched reactors and dispatching synchronous generation through hourly market signals — was designed for a network where synchronous mass provided natural damping and generators responded in seconds. In a network where **82% of generation consists of inverters that respond in milliseconds**, self- provide synchronism references via <GlossaryLink term="Phase-Locked Loop (PLL)">PLL</GlossaryLink>, and whose dynamic behaviour is opaque to the 400 kV SCADA, that paradigm has reached the limits of its management capacity.

28 April 2025 is not merely the case study of a blackout: it is the event that marks the **exhaustion of the centralised dispatch model** in systems with high power electronics penetration, and the mandatory starting point of a new architecture of distributed, real-time control for the 21st-century European grid.

<GlitchTitle>Communication Impact</GlitchTitle>

The 28 April blackout generated a second, parallel crisis alongside the electrical one: a communicative crisis whose consequences for public understanding of the incident persist well beyond supply restoration. This chapter analyses how media and social networks processed a technically complex phenomenon, and what gap opened between the expert reports' technical consensus and the narrative that reached the Spanish public.

## Institutional communication failure and the information vacuum

The voltage zero occurred at **12:33 CEST**. The first official public appearance by the head of government did not take place until **18:00 CEST** — more than **five hours later**. During that interval, a hyperconnected population, suddenly deprived of electricity and digital access, processed the emergency in the absence of any institutional interpretive framework.

This vacuum was immediately filled by what the specialist literature terms <GlossaryLink term="Crisis communication failure">crisis communication failure</GlossaryLink>: the inability of institutions to occupy the information space with verifiable technical messages during the critical post-incident window. The consequence was an episode of <GlossaryLink term="Infodemia">infodemia</GlossaryLink>: sabotage hypotheses, Russian cyberattack theories, anomalous atmospheric phenomena and governmental experiments with the power system circulated globally before system operators issued any preliminary diagnosis.

The nature of the incident made it especially vulnerable to this dynamic: a voltage collapse whose mechanics require knowledge of <GlossaryLink term="Estabilidad de tensión">voltage stability</GlossaryLink>, <GlossaryLink term="IBR">IBR</GlossaryLink> behaviour and <GlossaryLink term="OLTC (On-Load Tap Changer)">OLTC</GlossaryLink> dynamics is, by definition, **inversely proportional in accessibility** to the alternative explanations that replaced it in the public sphere.

The direct consequence was the incorporation of the incident into the political debate on the energy transition **before** any verified technical diagnosis existed. The Spanish public received for weeks causal explanations — «renewables caused the blackout», «there were not enough nuclear plants», «Europe abandoned Spain» — that the four technical reports **do not unanimously support**. The distance between the technical consensus and the dominant media narrative is itself one of the consequences of 28 April 2025, with direct implications for society's ability to evaluate the regulatory reforms the incident demonstrates are necessary.

## Press analysis: frames and technical biases

### Media critical of institutional management

Outlets such as El Mundo, ABC and La Razón articulated a narrative linking the collapse to the government's energy policy, interpreting the blackout as the foreseeable consequence of an energy transition that had prioritised intermittent sources without ensuring sufficient backup mechanisms.

Several arguments contain **verifiable inconsistencies** with the technical reports:

- **ABC** claimed the network was on the brink of collapse due to the «alarming lack of rotational inertia caused by shut-down nuclear plants». This directly contradicts the unanimous technical consensus of all four reports: official records certify that system <GlossaryLink term="Inercia (H)">inertia</GlossaryLink> was $H = 2.3$ s at the
  moment of collapse, above the ENTSO-E recommended threshold. The event was not
  an inertia-deficit collapse but a capacitive instability phenomenon.

- **El Mundo** ran «Flamanville 3 and France's 56 nuclear plants that saved anti-nuclear Sánchez during the great blackout», implicitly attributing supply restoration to nuclear technology. France's role in restoration was indeed significant — RTE activated up to 4,500 MW of support — but recovery was also underpinned by hydroelectric black start and Moroccan support, with nuclear generation as one of several factors.

- **La Razón** cited a preliminary report concluding that «the scheduling of insufficient synchronous generation with dynamic voltage control was the cause of the blackout». This finds **partial support** in the IIT-ICAI expert report: the reactive power absorption deficit in the southern zone was a documented factor. However, the same report notes that this deficit occurred in the context of the System Operator's meshing manoeuvres — a factor the coverage did not incorporate.

![Sample of front pages and publications from media critical of institutional management](/figuras/collage_conservador.png) _Figure 32. Representative coverage from media critical of the institutional response. A <GlossaryLink term="Encuadre mediático (Framing) y Agenda-shifting">framing</GlossaryLink> pattern is identifiable that reduces the multifactorial phenomenon to the relation «greater renewable penetration → less stability → blackout». Source: own compilation from X publications._

### Media favourable to the institutional narrative

Outlets aligned with the official narrative shifted focus toward REE's operational management, transmission network deficiencies and inherited policy. The organising premise was that the collapse was not a decarbonisation failure but the result of infrastructure not modernised at the required pace.

Some arguments are **technically consistent** with the reports:

- **El País** highlighted that exchange capacity with France stands at 3%, far below the EU 15% target. This argument is technically sound: greater interconnection capacity would have reduced the probability and severity of inter-area oscillations.

- **elDiario.es** noted that REE operated with reduced security margins despite forecasts of high solar irradiance and low synchronous generation. This is consistent with the reactive power deficit diagnosis in the south, though the coverage did not articulate the underlying Q-V curve saturation mechanism.

Deviations are also identified:

- **La Vanguardia** characterised the transpyrenean line opening as an «egotistical» act by continental mechanisms to safeguard French supply. This contradicts <GlossaryLink term="ENTSO-E">ENTSO-E</GlossaryLink>'s assessment: the 12:33:21
  CEST opening was the **automatic** actuation of Out-of-Step (OST)
  loss-of-synchronism protections in response to severe angular divergence.
  Attributing deliberate intent to an automatic protection mechanism confuses
  system protection operation with conscious operational decision-making.

- **infoLibre** published that private operators «deliberately» failed to absorb excess voltage. This incorporates the Government's «technical indiscipline» accusation but omits chronologically the first factor: the System Operator's meshing manoeuvre that injected capacitive reactive power into the network before any trip occurred.

![Sample publications from media favourable to the institutional narrative](/figuras/collage_progresista.png) _Figure 33. Representative coverage from media aligned with the official narrative. The evidence selection is symmetrically partial to that of the critical bloc: each media bloc incorporated facts consistent with its pre-existing frame and omitted those that contradicted it. Source: own compilation._

### International coverage: structural European framing

International press approached the blackout from a structural perspective. Not participating in the Spanish political debate, major international outlets framed the voltage zero as a systemic failure of European grid architecture and a warning for systems with high power electronics penetration.

![Sample international media coverage of the blackout](/figuras/collage_internacional.png) _Figure 34. International coverage of the incident. Outside the Spanish political debate, international media tended toward a structural European frame, with greater emphasis on critical infrastructure security arguments. Source: own compilation._

- **Reuters** provided the most technically rigorous analysis, highlighting interconnection capacity and the voltage support deficit from conventional plants in the moments before collapse.
- **Le Monde** took a descriptive approach to the cross-border impact.
- **BBC** focused on critical infrastructure security, documenting the safe shutdown of nuclear reactors and **refuting cyberattack hypotheses**.
- **Financial Times** ran «Spain and Portugal blackout blamed on solar power dependency», citing experts attributing instability to insufficient _«firm power»_. This does not match the technical consensus: the system had sufficient operational reserves and four coupled nuclear reactors. The event was not an active power collapse from generation shortage but a capacitive voltage instability phenomenon.
- **The Telegraph** suggested the Spanish government was conducting an «experiment» with the power system. This was refuted by Euronews Verify and Reuters Fact Check and found no support in any of the four technical reports.

### Synthesis: asymmetric evidence selection

The communication analysis concludes that the incident was largely not covered as a novel technical phenomenon but immediately framed within each outlet's pre-existing editorial interpretive framework:

- **Media critical of institutional management** emphasised synchronous generation deficit and energy policy as causes, frequently omitting the impact of the meshing manoeuvre.
- **Media favourable to the official narrative** emphasised operational error and interconnection deficits, frequently omitting actual generation fleet behaviour.

Neither bloc offered a representation of the technical multicausality as described in the expert reports. This dynamic carries implications beyond media analysis: the regulatory reforms identified as necessary —P.O. 7.4 update, deployment of <GlossaryLink term="Compensadores Síncronos (SynCons)">synchronous condensers</GlossaryLink>, transition to <GlossaryLink term="GFM (Grid-Forming)">grid-forming</GlossaryLink> mode — require sustained political consensus. Polarisation of the public debate around mutually exclusive causal narratives impedes the formation of that consensus.

## Social media response: three phases of collective uncertainty management

Analysis of activity on platform X during the blackout reveals a sequential evolution across three distinct phases.

### Phase 1 (0–6 hours): acute uncertainty and disinformation

The absence of government communication for the first five hours generated a process of <GlossaryLink term="Vacuum filling (Relleno del vacío informativo)">vacuum filling</GlossaryLink>: the information void was occupied by unverified sources. The high technical opacity of the overvoltage collapse favoured the propagation of sabotage hypotheses, cyberattack theories (the so-called «Operation Matryoshka») and atmospheric phenomena — all easily assimilated by the general public due to their externalising narratives.

Overlaid on this disinformation ecosystem, a citizen response emerged consistent with <GlossaryLink term="Emergent norm theory">emergent norm theory</GlossaryLink>: the development of collective coping mechanisms in the face of disruption. Everyday humour, irony and pragmatic normalisation functioned as collective emotional regulators during an unprecedented disruption.

![Citizen reactions on X during the first hours of the blackout](/figuras/collage_ciudadanos.png) *Citizen publications during the first hours. Three response patterns are identifiable: pragmatic normalisation and humour as a coping mechanism; institutional criticism through viral formats; and active search for causal explanations in the absence of official information. All three are consistent with emergent norm theory applied to digital environments during critical infrastructure disruptions. Source: X screenshots, own compilation.*

### Phase 2 (6–72 hours): politicisation and outrage communication

Following the official statement, digital discourse migrated toward responsibility attribution. This process corresponds to what crisis communication literature terms <GlossaryLink term="Outrage communication (Comunicación de indignación)">outrage communication</GlossaryLink>: indignation messages generate greater algorithmic diffusion capacity than technical explanations.

In the digital space critical of the government, the blackout was framed as evidence of poor management, with demands for resignations and accountability. In the space favourable to the institutional narrative, the argumentative line focused on positively evaluating the emergency response and defending the current energy model.

![Reactions from political figures on X during the 72 hours following the blackout](/figuras/collage_politicos.png) *Publications by Spanish political leaders on X during the 72 hours following the incident. None of the messages analysed addressed technical aspects of the overvoltage collapse, the <GlossaryLink term="Tap-Lag">Tap-Lag</GlossaryLink> phenomenon or the role of the meshing manoeuvre. Political communication from both positions was oriented towards responsibility attribution without incorporating the technical elements of the expert diagnosis. Source: X screenshots, own compilation.*

### Phase 3 (>72 hours): delayed correction with reduced reach

Verified technical explanations arrived with significantly lower reach than the initial messages. This reflects a structurally documented asymmetry: the temporal incompatibility between viral propagation speed and the inevitable slowness of technical forensic investigation.

### Synthesis: three structural asymmetries

The analysis identifies three structural asymmetries in the digital ecosystem when facing high technical complexity incidents:

1. **Temporal asymmetry**: viral propagation speed is incompatible with the pace of technical forensic investigation. The public receives hypotheses first and corrections later, with reduced reach.
2. **Vacuum asymmetry**: institutional information voids are not neutral — they are occupied by premature causal attributions that structure the subsequent debate.
3. **Algorithmic asymmetry**: political indignation messages have greater diffusion capacity than technical communication, regardless of their analytical precision.

These three asymmetries confirm that, in the face of technically complex electrical disruptions, public understanding is conditioned by each communicative agent's pre-existing interpretive frameworks, **regardless of the available technical evidence**. The consideration of this factor in the design of crisis communication protocols for critical systems operators constitutes one of the operational lessons of 28 April 2025.
