<GlitchTitle>Resilience & Future</GlitchTitle>

The structural lesson of 28 April does not reside in the collapse itself, but in the class of vulnerability it revealed. The forensic analysis demonstrated that the voltage zero was not a failure of active power reserves nor an isolated operational error: it was the terminal manifestation of a fundamental incompatibility between the physics of an inverter-dominated system and a technical-regulatory framework designed for synchronous networks. The scenario that produced the 28 April event — high <GlossaryLink term="IBR">IBR</GlossaryLink> penetration, scarce coupled synchronous generation and depressed net demand — was not a climatic anomaly, but a preview of conditions that will recur with increasing frequency as decarbonisation advances.

## The physics of systemic fragility

### Inertia, RoCoF and the swing equation

The dynamic frequency stability of a power system is governed by the **Swing Equation**:

$$
\frac{2H}{f_0} \, \frac{df}{dt} = P_m - P_e - D \cdot \Delta f
$$

where $H$ is the equivalent system inertia constant (in seconds), $f_0$ the nominal frequency (50 Hz), $df/dt$ the <GlossaryLink term="RoCoF (Rate of Change of Frequency)">RoCoF</GlossaryLink>, $P_m$ the total mechanical power input to coupled synchronous rotors, $P_e$ the net electrical power demanded and $D$ the damping coefficient of frequency-dependent loads.

The central parameter is $H$: its reduction means that any power imbalance translates into a proportionally sharper RoCoF, shortening the time window available for regulation systems to act. <GlossaryLink term="GFL (Grid-Following)">Grid-following</GlossaryLink> inverters are decoupled from the network frequency via their DC links and **contribute no inherent electromechanical inertia** to the swing equation.

The system certified $H = 2.3$ s at the moment of collapse — above the 2.0 s ENTSO-E recommended threshold. The 28 April event was not a frequency collapse from synchronous mass deficit. However, in scenarios with IBR penetration exceeding 80%, the sustained reduction of $H$ converts moderate-amplitude perturbations into critical contingencies, because the time available before <GlossaryLink term="UFLS (Underfrequency Load Shedding)">UFLS</GlossaryLink> relay activation compresses to the point where it becomes inoperable at the mechanical speed of breaker opening.

### Short-circuit power collapse: the network strength metric

The dimension most directly linked to the causal mechanism of 28 April is the degradation of short-circuit power ($S_{sc}$) at network nodes. A conventional synchronous generator can inject fault currents of **5 to 7 times** its nominal value during the first cycles of a transient. Inverters limit fault current injection to **1.1–1.2 p.u.** to prevent semiconductor burn-out.

The standard parametrisation of this loss is the Short Circuit Ratio (SCR):

$$
\mathrm{SCR} = \frac{S_{sc,\mathrm{PCC}}}{P_{\mathrm{IBR}}}
$$

<ForensicTable 
    title="TABLA 9 | SHORT CIRCUIT RATIO (SCR) THRESHOLDS"
    source="Estándar ENTSO-E / literatura técnica"
  >

| Category | SCR threshold | Operational implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Strong grid** | SCR > 3 | GFL inverters operate with small-signal stability. Distance protections maintain selectivity. |
| **Weak grid** | 2 ≤ SCR ≤ 3 | Degraded <GlossaryLink term="Phase-Locked Loop (PLL)">PLL</GlossaryLink> stability margin under fast perturbations. Risk of adverse control loop interaction between nearby installations. |
| **Very weak grid** | SCR &lt; 2 | GFL inverter PLLs prone to loss of synchronism under minor voltage variations. Distance protections lose directionality. |



</ForensicTable>

During the hours before the collapse, large areas of the Iberian Peninsula operated as **very weak grids** (SCR &lt; 2): massive solar production had displaced combined-cycle plants by merit order, removing precisely the $S_{sc}$ sources that provide nodal stiffness. Under these conditions, with $\mathrm{SCR} \ll 2$, the overall grid impedance becomes so high that voltage magnitude also becomes sensitive to <GlossaryLink term="Potencia activa">active power</GlossaryLink> variations: solar injection ramps acquire a voltage-disturbing power that would be harmless in conventional synchronous networks.

![Voltage maps of the peninsular 400 kV network during the critical pre-collapse period](/figuras/scr_iberia.png) _Figure 37. Geographical evolution of voltages in the 400 kV network prior to collapse (sequence a–d). Warm-colour zones show the progression and concentration of severe overvoltages in the southern and south-western peninsula — precisely the nodes with the greatest structural short-circuit power deficiency. Source: IIT-ICAI._

### The geometric paradox of inverters: P-Q conflict

There is a structural contradiction inherent to power triangle geometry. The maximum apparent capacity of an inverter is bounded by:

$$S_{\max} = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2}$$

When a photovoltaic plant experiences a sudden cloud clearing, its MPPT algorithms order active power injection ramps of thousands of MW/h. To avoid exceeding $S_{\max}$, the controller must simultaneously reduce its <GlossaryLink term="Potencia reactiva">reactive power</GlossaryLink> $Q$ margin. The paradox: that is precisely the moment when the abrupt increase in $P$ over a network with SCR &lt; 2 causes a severe overvoltage, requiring the inverter to massively absorb reactive power to contain it. The inverter faces two **simultaneously incompatible** physical obligations: maximise $P$ by market signal and maximise $Q$ for voltage stability.

This contradiction explains why 28 April was not an energy collapse but a control collapse: the system had sufficient resources but lacked the control architecture needed to deploy them coherently.

### The duck curve and the distributed self-consumption effect

The 28 April operating scenario sat in the **deep valley of the _duck curve_**: structurally low gross demand — analogous to minimums from two decades ago — with irradiance near summer maximums due to lower thermal cell degradation on a spring day.

![Evolution of coupled conventional synchronous units between 12h and 13h](/figuras/conventionalunits.png) _Figure 38. Conventional synchronous units coupled daily between 12h and 13h. The declining trend in the months preceding 28 April reflects systematic merit-order displacement — draining the system of electromechanical inertia at the critical moment. Source: ENTSO-E / own compilation._

By 12:30 CEST, REE had exhausted its manual management tools: preventive opening of dozens of extra-high-voltage lines to artificially increase series impedance, plus reactor operation at 85% capacity — without containing the voltage rise.

An additional factor identified as relevant was **distributed photovoltaic self-consumption**: distributed generation detracts visible demand without being telemetically observable at the required temporal resolution. During the pre-collapse oscillatory phenomena, voltage fluctuations activated anti-islanding relays at domestic and light industrial installations that disconnected en masse, suddenly revealing the demand these units had been covering: the effect was equivalent to an unanticipated positive load step, at a moment when the system already lacked reactive margin to absorb the resulting voltage drop.

## Zero-carbon enabling technologies

Overcoming the revealed vulnerability requires a transition in grid control architecture: from a generation fleet that _follows_ voltage and frequency to infrastructure capable of _forming_ them autonomously. Three complementary technology families articulate the response.

### BESS with grid-forming control: speed and precision

Unlike a GFL inverter, a <GlossaryLink term="GFM (Grid-Forming)">grid-forming</GlossaryLink> (GFM) inverter operates as a Thévenin equivalent: it autonomously synthesises an internal voltage reference in magnitude and angle ($V\angle\delta$) behind a virtual coupling impedance. By imposing this voltage vector instantaneously, the GFM inverter inherently injects or absorbs active and reactive current in response to any network variation, without depending on external phase measurements or calculation delays.

![Equivalent circuits of Grid-Following (GFL) and Grid-Forming (GFM) inverter topologies](/figuras/gfl_vs_gfm_circuit1.png) _Figure 39. Left: GFL inverter as a PLL-dependent controlled current source. Right: GFM inverter as an autonomous voltage source behind virtual impedance $Z_{\mathrm{GFM}}$. The fundamental difference: the GFM does not need to «read» the network to operate — it creates it._

When the GFM inverter is backed by a battery storage system (BESS-GFM), the combination delivers two additional stability services:

- **<GlossaryLink term="Inercia Sintética">Synthetic inertia</GlossaryLink>**: the algorithm continuously measures $df/dt$ and adjusts output power proportionally within **tens of milliseconds**, emulating rotating mass behaviour.
- **<GlossaryLink term="Fast Frequency Response (FFR)">FFR</GlossaryLink>**: upon exceeding a RoCoF or frequency deviation threshold, the BESS injects a predefined active power block **sub-cyclically** (≤ 0.25 s), arresting the frequency slope before synchronous governors can process the perturbation.

ERCOT (Texas) operational experience quantifies this service. The structural critical inertia threshold is approximately **100,000 MW·s**: below this, a category C contingency (~2,750 MW) drives frequency below 59.3 Hz before mechanical governors can act. The system operates with three alert zones: **green** (>120,000 MW·s), **yellow** (110,000–119,999 MW·s) and **red** (&lt;100,000 MW·s, with out-of-merit-order forced dispatch).

The RRS-FFR market requires: autonomous detection of drop below 59.85 Hz, injection of 100% contracted power within **0.25 s**, and 15-minute minimum maintenance. Verified results show that integrating **450 MW** under this FFR scheme reduced the critical inertia threshold from 100,000 MW·s to **88,000 MW·s** — a 12% reduction reflecting the functional equivalence between sub-second power electronics actuation and the kinetic mass of conventional synchronous machines.

However, IGBT semiconductors rarely sustain currents beyond **1.2–1.5 times** their nominal value. BESS-GFM contribution to available short-circuit power at a node is therefore quantitatively limited.

### Synchronous condensers: short-circuit power and genuine rotational inertia

The inverter current limitation justifies the complementary deployment of <GlossaryLink term="Compensadores Síncronos (SynCons)">synchronous condensers</GlossaryLink> (SynCons): large-mass rotating machines synchronously coupled to the network but operated unloaded, freely exchanging reactive power based on excitation level.

Their dual contribution: fault currents of the order of **300–400%** of nominal value during the first transient cycles, increasing the SCR at the connection node; and genuine rotational inertia physically available within the **first millisecond** of a transient, without algorithmic mediation or control latency.

The **<GlossaryLink term="Estrategia Brownfield">Brownfield strategy</GlossaryLink>** proposes a deployment path that minimises new civil investment: converting the large alternators of coal, combined-cycle or nuclear plants under decommissioning into synchronous condensers, once the turbine-generator set is decoupled. This converts stranded assets into systemic stability resources, preserving the value of already-installed 400 kV evacuation nodes.

### Hybrid architecture: complementarity as the condition of resilience

None of the three technology families, deployed in isolation, is sufficient:

- **BESS-GFM** deliver response speed, control precision and _Black Start_ capability, but are limited in short-circuit current.
- **SynCons** provide genuine rotational inertia and high short-circuit power, but lack the sub-cyclic agility of power electronics and do not manage active energy.
- **Synthetic inertia and FFR** maximise the battery energy margin utilisation, but depend on minimum nodal stiffness — provided by SynCons — for their control algorithms to be effective.

![Hybrid architecture for systemic resilience in decarbonised networks](/figuras/hitachi_hybrid.png) _Figure 40. Hybrid architecture scheme: BESS-GFM manage voltage in real time and deliver FFR; synchronous condensers provide rotational inertia and short-circuit power for nodal stiffness. Resilience requires both components — neither is a substitute for the other. Source: Hitachi Energy / FUTURED._

Minimising the total system cost does not coincide with minimising <GlossaryLink term="Coste Nivelado de la Energía (LCOE)">LCOE</GlossaryLink>, but requires internalising in market design the <GlossaryLink term="Servicios Esenciales de Confiabilidad (ERS)">Essential Reliability Services (ERS</GlossaryLink>) that synchronous machines provided implicitly.

![Techno-economic optimisation of resilience in IBR-dominated systems](/figuras/coste_optimo_ers.png) _Figure 41. The total system cost minimum is reached with a mix that remunerates ERS, not by simply maximising renewable penetration. The gap between the LCOE optimum and the system optimum is the cost of unrecompensed ancillary services. Source: Julia Matevosyan (ESIG) / FUTURED._

## The regulatory response: from obsolete P.O. 7.4 to mandatory grid-forming

### Pre-existing framework deficiencies

The P.O. 7.4 in force at the time of the blackout had not been substantially revised in approximately **twenty-five years**. It presented two critical deficiencies:

1. **Participation asymmetry**: 82% of the generation fleet operated at fixed power factor, unable to dynamically inject or absorb reactive power.
2. **Dead band**: synchronous generators were exempt from responding if voltage remained between 405 kV and 410 kV, creating a stepped response structurally incompatible with the speed of the documented capacitive transient.

![P.O. 7.4 original reactive power characteristic: dead band between 405 kV and 410 kV](/figuras/po74_banda_muerta.png) _The shaded zone illustrates the old P.O. 7.4 «dead band»: the range in which the generation fleet was not obliged to provide dynamic response, disabling system defence against fast capacitive transients. Source: REE._

### P.O. 7.4 revision, VOLTAIRE system and new remuneration scheme

The CNMC Resolution of 12 June 2025 (BOE-A-2025-13076) reformulated P.O. 7.4 under the new non-frequency services framework. The fundamental innovation is the replacement of static setpoint models with **remunerated dynamic delivery**: real-time setpoint tracking telemetrically sent by CECOEL through the CECRE.

The communication channel operates through the **VOLTAIRE** system: a two-layer hierarchical PI control loop. Tertiary Regulation optimises the national voltage profile globally via reactive optimal power flows. Secondary Regulation sends real-time telematic setpoints at a **4-second sampling resolution**, closing the control loop at park scale and eliminating dependence on manual operator response to low-amplitude voltage transients. This architecture transforms the renewable fleet's role: from passive consumer of grid voltage to **active actuator of the national regulation system**.

Associated remuneration includes **€2/MVArh** for real-time delivery during hours with positive net production; and for hours with zero or negative production — night-time periods where the Ferranti Effect on unloaded lines generates capacitive overvoltages — remuneration indexed to the Daily Average Market Price:

$$r_Q = 0.05 \times 1.15 \times \mathrm{PMD} + 5 \quad [€/\mathrm{MVArh}]$$

BESS systems additionally receive a capacity payment of **€2.7/MW/day**, conditional on maintaining a valid sample compliance rate above **90%**.

<ForensicTable 
    title="TABLA 10 | P.O. 7.4 REGULATORY FRAMEWORK COMPARISON"
    source="CNMC / REE"
  >

| Operational attribute | Original P.O. 7.4 (pre-2025) | Updated framework (post-2025) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Control nature | Static and asymmetric. Discrete step operation. | Dynamic, continuous and proportional to deviation. |
| IBR participation | Passive _grid-following_ at fixed power factor. | _Grid-forming_ mandatory. Active control of $V$ and $Q$. |
| Dead band ($V$) | 405–410 kV with no mandatory response. | Eliminated or reduced to ±0.5% of $U_n$. |
| Reactive response | Slow setpoint steps following OS request. | Automatic closed-loop response (_droop control_). |
| Q remuneration | Based on declared technical availability. | Zonal ERS market mechanisms. |
| Observability | SCADA telemetry at 400 kV, multi-second resolution. | PMU and 4-second telemetry for distributed IBR. |
| Sanctions | No specific penalties for reactive setpoint non-compliance. | Financial penalties for failure to maintain 90% minimum compliance rate. |



</ForensicTable>

**Royal Decree 997/2025** complemented the reform with four urgent measures: legal redefinition of BESS as systemic stability service assets; sanitisation of the obsolete connection permit register; mandatory telemetry at &lt; 4 s resolution for all significant IBR; and mandatory PSS/POD oscillation damping module for all new GFM inverters > 10 MW.

A revealing regulatory tension emerged in October 2025: REE requested raising the compliance threshold from 75% to 90% of the time. The CNMC denied it, citing the **technical impossibility of existing synchronous units** to achieve that level with the required adjustment ramps. The finding is significant in the opposite direction: GFM inverters could meet that requirement without difficulty. The adaptation of the operating framework to IBR-GFM capabilities is advancing faster than that of the synchronous assets it replaces as ancillary service providers.

### The European framework: NC RfG 2.0 and ENTSO-E Phase I and II reports

The <GlossaryLink term="NC RfG">NC RfG</GlossaryLink> in force over the last decade was designed under the GFL paradigm: it standardised fault ride-through profiles and frequency thresholds, but did not contemplate the possibility that no heavy rotating machine remained to follow. This conceptual gap was demonstrated in the 8 seconds of the Iberian collapse.

ENTSO-E's Technical Group on Grid-Forming Capability (TG GFC) produced two reference documents:

- **Phase I Report (May 2024)**: Established the fundamental GFM technical definition required by the new code — «voltage source behind a constant effective reactance» during the first milliseconds after a perturbation. This phasor model de facto proscribes direct PLL algorithm dependencies for primary fault current control.
- **Phase II Report (November 2025)**: Published under the weight of the Iberian collapse evidence, with cross-endorsement from CENELEC, WindEurope, SolarPower Europe and EASE. Establishes definitively how new inverter-based generation and storage must stabilise the system.

The **NC RfG 2.0** obligations are applied with a technology-agnostic approach, classifying modules into four types:

<ForensicTable 
    title="TABLA 11 | NC RFG 2.0 (PROPOSED) COMPLIANCE TIERS"
    source="ENTSO-E / Comisión Europea"
  >

| Type | Power / Connection | GFM requirement | Timeline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Type A** | &lt; 1 MW | Voluntary. DSO discretion. | N/A |
| **Type B** | 1–50 MW | Mandatory. Synthetic inertia and basic dynamic voltage support. | Max. 3 years after ENTSO-E IGD publication. |
| **Type C** | > 50 MW | Mandatory and comprehensive. Full voltage source operation; fault current profiles; POD functionality. | 3 years after European Commission adoption. |
| **Type D** | ≥ 110 kV or > 75 MW | As Type C plus certification testing. | 3 years after European Commission adoption. |
| **ESM (BESS)** | Per category | As equivalent PPM. V2G systems with combined capacity > 1 MW classified as ESM Type B. | Per category. |



</ForensicTable>

As of the writing of this work, formal adoption of NC RfG 2.0 by the European Commission **is deprioritised with no official timeline**, creating a regulatory uncertainty window that national operators are managing through preventive measures outside the code.

## Essential Reliability Services (ERS) markets

### The headroom problem: why energy markets do not remunerate stability

For a GFM inverter to act as a voltage source under severe RoCoF or voltage perturbations, it must mandatorily maintain an unused reserve of its apparent capacity ($S_{\max}$) in steady state. This reserve — the **_headroom_** — requires either deliberately limiting active power injected into the daily energy market, or oversizing the IGBT power stage, drastically increasing CAPEX. Without direct economic compensation, neither option is commercially viable.

The structural failure of the pre-28 April regulatory architecture resided in its punitive focus: penalising technical deviations without remunerating firmness attributes. ERS markets correct this asymmetry.

### Three remuneration mechanisms

**1. Regional synthetic inertia and FFR markets.** Design will advance towards auctions paying a capacity or availability fee to assets capable of providing inertial support in margins &lt; 5 ms. The mechanism's logic is **_revenue stacking_**: BESS systems receive simultaneous income from daily energy market arbitrage, frequency regulation auctions (aFRR/mFRR), and capacity payments for synthetic inertia and FFR. This income multiplicity compensates high CAPEX from oversizing and income loss from reactive _headroom_.

**2. Geographic short-circuit level signals.** Unlike frequency — a global metric — SCR and overvoltages are **radically local** phenomena. The vulnerable nodes of 28 April do not coincide with the highest installed power density nodes. ERS markets will adopt granular spatial price signals: discounted connection tariffs or reactive capacity auctions at peripheral nodes mathematically identified by TSOs as SCR &lt; 2 enclaves. BESS-GFM placement at the correct nodes becomes determinative for project economic viability, as ERS service prices will be locally higher in zones of greater systemic fragility.

**3. Ex-ante remuneration for SynCons.** For infrastructure such as SynCons — which provide pure physical inertia and massive fault currents but cannot sell energy in the hourly market — regulation contemplates _Rate of Return Regulation_ models without energy price risk exposure, or long-term adjudications that shield capital investment and assure the System Operator a reliable rotating base irrespective of instantaneous IBR-GFM penetration.

![Revenue stacking diagram for a BESS-GFM system under the post-28A regulatory framework](/figuras/ers_revenue_stacking.png) _Stacked income sources for a BESS-GFM system: daily energy market, frequency balance markets (aFRR/mFRR), synthetic inertia and FFR auctions, and ERS reactive availability payments. Income multiplicity compensates the required technical oversizing. Source: own elaboration based on ENTSO-E structure._

### Reference models: EirGrid DS3 and ERCOT RRS-FFR

EirGrid (Ireland) and ERCOT (Texas) are the proven operational references towards which European ERS market design is converging: both operators have faced in advance the challenges of non-synchronous penetration above 75%.

EirGrid's **DS3** programme fragmented stability provision into 14 specialised products. The three most relevant for the 28 April context:

<ForensicTable 
    title="TABLA 12 | EIRGRID DS3 SERVICES - CORE PARAMETERS"
    source="EirGrid / ENTSO-E"
  >

| Service | Technical definition | Threshold / Window |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Synchronous Inertial Response (SIR)** | Near-instantaneous provision of active power and synchronising torque under frequency drops. Remunerated via SIRF = $E_k / P_{\min}$ index, penalising dispatch of inefficient plants injecting unwanted power solely to contribute marginal inertia. | SIRF ≥ 15 s |
| **Fast Frequency Response (FFR)** | Rapid active power injection following an abrupt frequency drop event. Validated energy is the integral of additional injected power in the first 10 s ($T_0 \to T{+}10\,\mathrm{s}$). Provided energy must be strictly greater than recovery energy loss ($T{+}10\,\mathrm{s} \to T{+}20\,\mathrm{s}$). | Response between 0.15 s and 2 s |
| **Steady-State Reactive Power (SSRP)** | Total despatchable reactive power range ($Q_{\mathrm{range}}$, in MVAr) that the inverter can inject or absorb continuously across its full active power range. Includes a favourable remuneration scalar for IBR capable of providing reactive power at no load (_watt-less VARs_). | Steady state; annual valuation via PLEXOS models |



</ForensicTable>

The comparison between DS3 and RRS-FFR suggests a **two-layer ERS market architecture** for the European context: a layer of geographic short-circuit signals — analogous to EirGrid's SSRP — and a sub-cyclic frequency response layer — analogous to ERCOT's RRS-FFR.

### Evolution of the Spanish framework in 2026

On 8 May 2026, the CNMC opened a public hearing procedure for the modification of Operating Procedures P.O. 7.4 and P.O. 14.4 (File DCOOR/DE/006/26), oriented towards the creation of zonal non-frequency service markets with active IBR and BESS participation.

The structural lesson that 28 April 2025 inscribes in European regulatory design has broader scope than any incremental adjustment to operating procedures: the physical attributes that synchronous systems provided inherently — inertia, short-circuit power, autonomous voltage control — **have ceased to be free externalities** and have become services whose provision must be explicitly defined, verified and remunerated. The pure marginalist energy model is structurally incapable of remunerating these attributes. Without that economic translation of resilience, no NC RfG 2.0 technical requirement will prove sustainable in the medium term.

<GlitchTitle>Consecuencias Financieras y Costes de Resiliencia: Auditoría Económica</GlitchTitle>

El colapso sistémico de la red eléctrica de la península ibérica, materializado el 28 de abril de 2025 a las 12:33 horas (CEST), representa uno de los eventos de disrupción de infraestructuras críticas más severos en la historia económica contemporánea de la Unión Europea. Con una pérdida instantánea de **31 gigavatios (GW)** de carga, la desconexión abrupta de los sistemas de España y Portugal de la red síncrona continental, y la afectación directa a más de **50 millones de ciudadanos** y la totalidad del tejido productivo peninsular, las ramificaciones de este suceso trascienden la fenomenología puramente electromecánica. 

Este evento, catalogado por la Red Europea de Gestores de Redes de Transporte de Electricidad (ENTSO-E) como inédito y multifactorial, ha expuesto vulnerabilidades estructurales profundas en el diseño del mercado energético, la planificación de la transición ecológica y los esquemas de contingencia regulatoria.

El presente informe técnico despliega una auditoría financiera y macroeconómica de carácter exhaustivo, estructurada para desentrañar y cuantificar las repercusiones directas del cero de tensión, la subsiguiente onda expansiva de litigiosidad y expedientes sancionadores, y el coste ineludible de la adaptación tecnológica estructural (CAPEX) requerida para mitigar el riesgo de futuros eventos de riesgo de cola (*tail-risk*). 

A través del prisma de la economía de la energía y la auditoría de infraestructuras críticas, la premisa analítica fundamental que rige este documento demuestra axiomáticamente que **el coste del capital destinado a la resiliencia sistémica es órdenes de magnitud inferior a la masiva destrucción de valor** (OPEX sobrevenido, lucro cesante e indemnizaciones cruzadas) generada por la vulnerabilidad de la red.

---

## 1. El Coste Directo del Apagón (Pérdidas Inmediatas y Macroeconomía)

La evaluación rigurosa de las pérdidas económicas inmediatas derivadas de un colapso eléctrico no puede restringirse exclusivamente a la facturación no realizada por las empresas generadoras y distribuidoras. Por el contrario, exige un análisis de equilibrio general que parametrice el impacto paralizante sobre el Producto Interior Bruto (PIB) de la región afectada durante el lapso de interrupción generalizada. Para la articulación de este cálculo, la ortodoxia de la economía de la energía impone la utilización de la métrica del **Valor de la Energía No Suministrada (VoLL, por sus siglas en inglés: Value of Lost Load)**.

### Análisis del Valor de la Energía No Suministrada (VoLL) en la Economía Ibérica

El VoLL constituye el estándar regulatorio y académico —avalado por la Agencia de Cooperación de los Reguladores de la Energía (ACER) y el Consejo de Reguladores Europeos de la Energía (CEER)— para estimar el precio marginal máximo que los consumidores estarían dispuestos a abonar (*Willingness to Pay - WTP*) para evitar una interrupción del suministro, o alternativamente, la compensación exigida (*Willingness to Accept - WTA*) por sufrir dicho corte. Funciona como una aproximación monetaria directa al excedente marginal del consumidor asociado a la continuidad y seguridad de la infraestructura eléctrica.

Durante el apagón del 28 de abril de 2025, la península ibérica se enfrentó a un cero absoluto de tensión que desconectó súbitamente 25,2 GW de carga base y pico. La restitución del suministro operó bajo una dinámica asimétrica y gradual; mientras que para las 19:00 horas del mismo día se había logrado restablecer el 35% de la demanda, vastas áreas industriales y metropolitanas no recuperaron la normalidad operativa hasta la madrugada del 29 de abril, transcurriendo en algunos nodos hasta **14 horas de blackout ininterrumpido** y finalizando los trabajos técnicos a las 14:36 horas del día 29.

Para parametrizar el coste macroeconómico agregado, es imperativo desglosar el VoLL por segmentos sectoriales, dada la profunda heterogeneidad en la dependencia energética, la resiliencia de los procesos y la elasticidad del daño financiero frente al tiempo de interrupción. Las metodologías econométricas de la Unión Europea y los estudios de fallas (*Blackout Studies*) establecen las siguientes horquillas valorativas para economías desarrolladas equivalentes a la española y portuguesa.

<ForensicTable
  title="TABLE 13 | VoLL ESTIMATES BY SECTOR"
  source="Own elaboration (VoLL model)"
>

| Macroeconomic Sector | Estimated VoLL Range (€/kWh) | Marginal Sensitivity to Disruption | Second-Order Impact (*Ripple Effects*) on the Economy |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Residential / Domestic** | 5.00 - 45.00 | Low-Medium (Increases exponentially with duration) | Loss of thermal comfort, deterioration of perishable inventories, massive disruption of labor productivity due to the drop in telecommuting and communications. |
| **Services / Retail Trade** | 15.00 - 90.00 | Medium-High (Extreme sensitivity during daytime hours) | Forced closure of commercial establishments, absolute paralysis of payment gateways and POS terminals, logistical and data server collapse in the tertiary sector. |
| **Industrial (General Manufacturing)** | 50.00 - 250.00 | Very High (Chain processes) | Supply shortages in production lines, loss of raw materials due to non-sequenced stops, damage to capital equipment due to voltage transients, and breakdown of Just-in-Time supply chains. |

</ForensicTable>

Tomando en consideración la curva de demanda real, programada y prevista para el día 28 de abril, y calculando la integral del área bajo la curva desde las 12:33 horas (momento del colapso) hasta el restablecimiento progresivo del 99,95% de la demanda a las 07:00 horas del 29 de abril, la Energía No Suministrada (ENS) agregada para el sistema ibérico se sitúa de forma conservadora en el espectro de los **150.000 a 180.000 Megavatios-hora (MWh)**, es decir, entre 150 y 180 GWh. *(Nota metodológica: La horquilla de 150–180 GWh refleja la incertidumbre en la estimación del consumo elástico destruido versus desplazado. El límite inferior asume recuperación parcial de carga industrial nocturna; el superior asume destrucción neta por parada fría de procesos)*.

La aplicación de un VoLL medio ponderado —que internaliza la paralización concurrente del sector primario, secundario y terciario en un día laborable (lunes)— proyecta un impacto financiero devastador. Las auditorías y estimaciones preliminares elaboradas por corporaciones como la CEOE y ATA convergieron en situar la destrucción directa e indirecta de valor en la horquilla de los **1.000 a 1.500 millones de euros**. Esta cifra, congruente con el modelo analítico del VoLL, expone que la carencia coyuntural de un bien cuyo precio de mercado diario oscilaba en niveles deprimidos (18,50 €/MWh en el pool antes del apagón) provocó externalidades negativas multimillonarias.

Este impacto macroeconómico se vio amplificado de manera sistémica por el colapso colateral de los servicios de telecomunicaciones e internet. Las métricas de enrutamiento global evidenciaron que, en el instante del apagón, el tráfico de internet en Portugal continental se desplomó inicialmente a la mitad, cayendo hasta un 90% en las cinco horas subsiguientes respecto a la línea base histórica, lo que arrastró consigo a ecosistemas financieros, plataformas fintech y operativas cloud transnacionales, originando un lucro cesante intangible de proporciones masivas.

### Distorsión de Precios en el Mercado Mayorista (OMIE) y el PVPC

La crisis de infraestructura provocó un cisma financiero inmediato en el mercado diario e intradiario gestionado por el Operador del Mercado Ibérico de Energía (OMIE). En la fase temporal inmediatamente anterior al colapso, concretamente en la mañana del 28 de abril, el mercado mostraba claros síntomas de sobreoferta renovable; el precio marginal se situaba en niveles anormalmente bajos, promediando apenas **5,79 euros por megavatio hora (MWh)**, e incluso registrando tramos horarios con precios nulos o marginalmente negativos (donde el sistema remuneraba hasta 10 €/MWh por la retirada de energía).

No obstante, la reconstrucción topológica de la red posterior al apagón (*black-start*) y la necesidad imperativa de inyectar inercia rotacional y control de tensión forzaron al operador del sistema (REE) a alterar drásticamente la jerarquía del despacho económico. El restablecimiento exigió marginar parcialmente la generación renovable e hidroeléctrica, recurriendo de urgencia a las centrales térmicas de ciclo combinado de gas natural. Al dictar el gas el precio marginal de casación, el coste de la electricidad en el mercado mayorista experimentó un incremento exponencial, multiplicándose por cinco de manera casi instantánea frente a los niveles pre-apagón.

Este encarecimiento no operó en el vacío, sino que se trasladó con suma celeridad a los consumidores, especialmente a aquellos indexados al Precio Voluntario para el Pequeño Consumidor (PVPC). Los sobrecostes originados por las restricciones técnicas necesarias para mantener el sistema a flote tras el apagón provocaron que los clientes regulados experimentaran un **incremento del 125%** en el componente específico de restricciones de su factura, materializándose en un aumento medio estructural de más de 3 euros mensuales por hogar y trasladando un coste sistémico ineficiente a los estratos de consumidores vulnerables.

---

## 2. El Impacto del Deslastre Automático en los Consumidores Electrointensivos

Más allá del sector comercial y residencial, el epicentro del daño material directo recayó sobre el tejido industrial pesado. Ante la caída incontrolada de la frecuencia y la tensión, los automatismos de la red activaron protocolos de supervivencia extrema, desencadenando el deslastre automático de cargas. Este mecanismo de seccionamiento de emergencia, diseñado para aislar nodos y evitar el daño en la red de transporte de muy alta tensión (400 kV), operó como una guillotina operativa para la industria.

Los consumidores electrointensivos, caracterizados por mantener procesos de termodinámica crítica en flujo continuo ininterrumpido (siderurgia, metalurgia, electrólisis, refino), sufrieron disrupciones operativas letales. La Asociación de Empresas con Gran Consumo de Energía (AEGE), que aglutina a gigantes como Acerinox, ArcelorMittal, Asturiana de Zinc (Azsa), Ercros y Grupo Gallardo Balboa, reportó pérdidas financieras auditadas superiores a los **25 millones de euros** derivados de este evento aislado.

Este sumatorio delata la fragilidad del CAPEX industrial frente a las perturbaciones de la red y se estructura en dos vectores de pérdida claramente diferenciados:

1. **Daños Operativos Directos (Estimados en más de 13 millones de euros):** La supresión súbita de la alimentación eléctrica sin rampa de parada controlada provocó colapsos térmicos masivos. En plantas metalúrgicas, la interrupción en hornos de arco eléctrico originó la solidificación de metales líquidos en crisoles y líneas de colada, destruyendo revestimientos refractarios. La reactivación de estas líneas implicó jornadas completas dedicadas exclusivamente a la limpieza industrial, retirada de escoria endurecida y sustitución de bienes de equipo quemados por los transitorios de tensión generados en el instante del deslastre.
2. **Lucro Cesante y Costes de Oportunidad (Estimados en 12 millones de euros):** Si bien la interrupción neta del suministro en ciertos polígonos osciló entre las cuatro y las catorce horas, la inercia termodinámica de estos procesos es implacable. El encendido, precalentamiento y recalibración de las líneas de producción supuso, en términos prácticos, "pérdidas de varios días después", aniquilando la capacidad de las factorías para cumplir con las entregas pautadas (*Just-In-Time*), e induciendo penalizaciones en los contratos de suministro internacionales.

Desde una óptica macroeconómica superior, la falta de una arquitectura de red capaz de garantizar el suministro y la incapacidad de establecer compensaciones ágiles han erosionado drásticamente el capital reputacional de España y Portugal. El riesgo operativo de sufrir paradas no programadas supera financieramente cualquier descuento horario en el megavatio-hora, demostrando que la seguridad de suministro es el pilar innegociable de la política industrial.

---

## 3. El Coste Legal y Regulador (Sanciones y Litigiosidad)

Los efectos del apagón del 28 de abril se extendieron más allá de la resincronización de los alternadores, derivando en un complejo escenario institucional y jurídico. Lo que la ENTSO-E diagnosticó como una avería originada por un fallo técnico "inédito, imprevisible y multifactorial", motivó a nivel doméstico diversas auditorías y demandas mercantiles cruzadas.

### Expedientes Sancionadores de la CNMC

Operando bajo sus prerrogativas como organismo supervisor de cumplimiento normativo (*ex-post*), la Dirección de Instrucción de Energía de la Comisión Nacional de los Mercados y la Competencia (CNMC) lanzó una campaña de escrutinio sin precedentes. Argumentando la existencia de un ecosistema de indisciplina técnica entre los actores del mercado, la CNMC desplegó una investigación forense que analizó la telemetría operativa de los dos años previos al evento, culminando en la incoación de hasta **66 expedientes sancionadores**.

Estos procedimientos administrativos impactaron contra el núcleo duro del oligopolio eléctrico y gestor de infraestructuras: Iberdrola, Endesa, Naturgy, Repsol y el propio operador del sistema, Red Eléctrica de España (REE). Los cargos principales orbitaron en torno a indicios de incumplimientos continuados en las normativas de programación diaria, desviaciones en las consignas de control dinámico de tensión y la deficiente inyección/absorción de potencia reactiva.

De singular relevancia jurídica y técnica fue la apertura de un expediente calificado como "grave" contra Mercuria Sostenible, entidad gestora de la Infraestructura Común de Evacuación (ICE) emplazada en la subestación de Huéneja, en la provincia de Granada. Esta investigación situó a la promoción de energías renovables en el foco del huracán regulatorio, pues los análisis topológicos del apagón señalaron dicha subestación como el "punto cero", funcionando como una inmensa regleta colectora donde la falta de mitigación de sobretensiones propició la primera desconexión en cascada masiva de plantas fotovoltaicas, eólicas y termosolares.

El marco punitivo desplegado por la CNMC se ancla estrictamente en el articulado de la Ley 24/2013, del Sector Eléctrico (LSE), revelando contingencias financieras formidables para los balances de las *utilities*:
- **Infracciones "Graves":** Tipificadas bajo los artículos 64.15, 64.16 y 64.17 de la LSE, conllevan sanciones pecuniarias con un techo máximo de **6 millones de euros** por expediente.
- **Infracciones "Muy Graves":** Sustentadas bajo preceptos como el artículo 64.37 y el artículo 61.a (poner en riesgo manifiesto la garantía de suministro). El castigo financiero estipulado para estas faltas asciende hasta un límite máximo de **60 millones de euros** por infracción.

### Litigiosidad Mercantil por Daños y Competencia Desleal

En paralelo a las actuaciones administrativas, la necesidad de depurar responsabilidades derivó en litigios entre las grandes corporaciones, evidenciando el peso económico del "riesgo reputacional" en el mercado energético. Un caso paradigmático ha sido la interposición de una demanda civil por parte del grupo Iberdrola contra el gestor de la red de transporte Red Eléctrica (REE) y su sociedad matriz, Redeia Corporación, sustentada en la Ley de Competencia Desleal.

La génesis de este litigio se halla en las manifestaciones proferidas por la cúpula ejecutiva de Redeia durante el periodo de crisis, donde argumentó que REE ejecutó "5.000 maniobras impecables" y deslizó responsabilidades hacia el comportamiento anómalo de la red de generación renovable y el autoconsumo, apuntando de forma directa a ineficiencias críticas en el control de tensión de la magna planta fotovoltaica Núñez de Balboa, propiedad de Iberdrola.

Iberdrola estructuró una audaz estrategia legal, eludiendo la vía contencioso-administrativa, para incardinar el conflicto en la jurisdicción civil ordinaria. Iberdrola argumentó con contundencia que las declaraciones públicas emanadas desde la cúpula directiva de REE resultaron inexactas, parciales e innecesariamente despectivas, construyendo una narrativa mediática que transfirió injustamente la responsabilidad del cero nacional a la gestión privada de la eléctrica, devaluando el prestigio de la compañía frente a sus accionistas y penalizando coyunturalmente su valor bursátil.

---

## 4. El Coste de las Reformas Obligatorias (CAPEX: Retrofitting y Nuevo P.O. 7.4)

El análisis forense del colapso ibérico expuso de manera incontrovertible la obsolescencia técnica de una red de transporte que ha transicionado aceleradamente hacia una alta penetración de electrónica de potencia distribuida incapaces, bajo la regulación previa, de sostener parámetros críticos como la tensión y la inercia rotacional pura.

### La Sostenibilidad Financiera y la "Operación Reforzada" (El OPEX Tóxico)

Como parche de contención de emergencia inmediatamente posterior al apagón, Red Eléctrica instauró la denominada **"Operación Reforzada"**. Esta doctrina operativa restringe severamente la participación de energías renovables en el mercado diario, forzando la programación centralizada y masiva de plantas de generación síncrona. Así, el sistema pasó de contar con unas 7 centrales de ciclo combinado de gas activadas en régimen normal, a mantener entre 25 y 30 centrales quemando gas natural de manera constante para proveer la firmeza, inercia y capacidad de cortocircuito.

Desde una perspectiva de contabilidad analítica, la Operación Reforzada se ha erigido como un agujero negro financiero. Las propias estimaciones corporativas de Redeia cifraron el coste directo de este sobreesfuerzo en **711 millones de euros** únicamente para los doce meses posteriores al incidente. Sin embargo, auditorías externas desarrolladas por consultoras globales como PwC escalaron la magnitud real del daño sistémico, estimando un sobrecoste superior a los **1.000 millones de euros** respecto al ejercicio 2024.

Este sumatorio de ineficiencias (OPEX) no aporta ningún valor añadido patrimonial a la red; es puramente gasto corriente para mantener el sistema a flote. Agrava el déficit comercial de la balanza de pagos española, dispara los derechos de emisión de CO2, y desincentiva la inversión al provocar un incremento masivo de vertidos renovables (*curtailment*).

### El Retrofitting del Parque Renovable y el Nuevo P.O. 7.4

El primer pilar de la reestructuración se formalizó con la promulgación del nuevo **Procedimiento de Operación 7.4 (P.O. 7.4)**, denominado *"Servicio complementario de control de tensión de la red de transporte"*.

Esta profunda revisión regulatoria exige, con carácter retroactivo y obligatorio, que las instalaciones de régimen especial basadas en electrónica de potencia dejen de operar como meros inyectores pasivos de potencia activa (P), asumiendo obligaciones de modulación dinámica. La normativa impele a estos nodos a inyectar o absorber potencia reactiva (Q) para sostener el perfil de tensión y responder a huecos de tensión (LVRT/HVRT).

Para cumplir esta exigencia, las promotoras se ven obligadas a invertir capital en la reingeniería de la planta: instalando arquitecturas de Controladores Lógicos de Planta (PPC), adicionando bancos de capacitores estáticos (STATCOMs) o sobredimensionando físicamente las bahías de inversores modulares. Asumiendo que la mitad del parque requerirá modificaciones de hardware, y estimando un *Unit Cost* de actualización de entre 5.000 y 15.000 euros por megavatio instalado, **la factura de retrofitting agregada a nivel nacional oscilará entre los 400 y los 1.000 millones de euros**.

### Inversión Estructural: Condensadores Síncronos y Baterías BESS a Gran Escala

El control de reactiva propuesto por el P.O. 7.4 es una condición necesaria pero insuficiente. El ecosistema requiere de un segundo pilar de CAPEX: la inserción estratégica de sistemas híbridos combinando Baterías de Almacenamiento de Energía a Gran Escala (BESS) con Condensadores Síncronos (*Synchronous Condensers*) en los nodos de la red de transporte con mayor nivel de congestión (Extremadura y Andalucía).

Un condensador síncrono es un gigantesco generador rotativo acoplado a la red cuyo eje gira en vacío. Su masa rotacional proporciona inercia sintética pura y una capacidad de respuesta instintiva frente a corrientes de cortocircuito.

Basado en proyectos piloto reales (como el acuerdo corporativo en 2026 entre Engie y Rolwind en Andalucía para 278 MW de potencia y 1,1 GWh de almacenamiento), el coste paramétrico es de aproximadamente **0,86 Millones de Euros por MW de capacidad instalada**.

Para que el operador del sistema (REE) prescinda de la sobreprogramación de gas que sustenta la "Operación Reforzada", se requiere la instalación de un mínimo operativo de entre **3.000 y 4.000 MW**.

**Estimación del CAPEX Estructural a Nivel Nacional:**

$$
3.500 \text{ MW} \times 0,86 \text{ M€/MW} \approx 3.010 \text{ Millones de Euros}
$$

Bajo el régimen tarifario post-apagón, el OPEX despilfarrado en el coste de restricciones técnicas impuestas por la "Operación Reforzada" asciende a más de 1.000 millones. En un modelo básico de evaluación financiera, un CAPEX de 3.000 millones de euros para dotar de inercia limpia a la red tendría un periodo de retorno de inversión dinámico (*Payback*) menor a cinco años. El Valor Actual Neto (VAN) del proyecto es masivamente positivo.

---

## 5. Conclusiones Contractuales: La Resiliencia como Inversión Rentable

La radiografía forense del Gran Apagón del 28 de abril de 2025 trasciende la estricta naturaleza del incidente electromecánico para conformar un evento de cisma macroeconómico. El balance contable agregado de la catástrofe eléctrica es inapelable:

- La asfixia de caja del sector electrointensivo (>25 M€).
- La destrucción de valor macroeconómico por el lucro cesante de la Energía No Suministrada (VoLL), estimado entre **1.000 y 1.500 millones de euros**.
- La guerra judicial derivada y las multas coercitivas de la CNMC.
- El OPEX reaccionario superior a **711 millones de euros anuales** mediante la quema de gas natural de la "Operación Reforzada".

Frente a la constante hemorragia en la balanza de pagos del sistema eléctrico, el esfuerzo inversor para la modernización integral del ecosistema (entre 3.000 y 3.500 M€ en CAPEX para Condensadores Síncronos y retrofitting del P.O 7.4) no debe ser conceptuado como un pasivo gubernamental, sino como un escudo fiscal estratégico. Invertir ingentes capitales *ex-ante* en la robustez física y algorítmica de la red no solo es el seguro más barato imaginable, sino la prerrogativa absoluta para salvaguardar la soberanía industrial y asegurar el éxito irreversible de la transición energética.

title: "Uso de Inteligencia Artificial"

<GlitchTitle>Use of Artificial Intelligence</GlitchTitle>

This thesis was developed under an atypical methodological context: the simultaneous occurrence, during 2024–2026, of a systemic crisis in the Iberian power system and an accelerated transformation in natural language processing tools. The availability of Large Language Models (LLMs) capable of processing hundreds of pages of technical documentation within minutes coincided with the publication, within a single year, of four primary expert reports and a dozen academic analyses of the same event. This chapter transparently documents how these tools were integrated, what specific tasks they performed, what systematic errors were detected and corrected, and what epistemological reflection this experience yields for engineering research practice.

## Methodological application: five operational functions

The initial documentary body encompasses technical dossiers, ENTSO-E regulations, official reports exceeding 200 pages, IIT-ICAI PSS/E simulations, CNMC proceedings, NREL oscillographic records and a substantial volume of specialist press. Linear reading without computational mediation was incompatible with the TFG's academic timeline. Generative model integration was structured around five clearly delineated operational functions, **none of which involves autonomous causal inference about system physics**:

<ForensicTable 
    title="TABLA 14 | LLM ASSISTANCE — OPERATIONAL FUNCTIONS"
    source="Elaboración propia"
  >

| Function | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **Chronological reconciliation** | The four reports describe the same physical events of 28 April with different temporal granularity and occasional discrepancies of up to 200 ms between versions. Automated assistance enabled construction of a unified master _timestamp_ table that served as scaffolding for Chapters 3 and 4. |
| **Systematic divergence mapping** | Each report frames the incident within a distinct analytical perimeter. Assisted extraction of homologous passages allowed the identification of technically incompatible claims between sources — the basis of Chapter 5 and the comparative synthesis. |
| **Quantitative tabulation** | Consolidation of magnitudes distributed across reports: zonal inertia values, instantaneous renewable penetration, cross-border exchanges, UFLS figures, meshing manoeuvre capacitive contributions. |
| **Editorial support** | Suggestion of lexical variants, synonym resolution, terminology control and reformulation of dense academic prose passages. This support **did not alter the argumentative structure or content decisions**, which remain the author's exclusive responsibility. |
| **Graphical element scaffolding** | Generation of TikZ and `pgfplots` drafts from textual descriptions, subsequently reviewed, refined and manually validated for visual consistency and data fidelity. |



</ForensicTable>

The workflow is structured in three sequential stages with a correction loop:

[Primary sources] → [LLM assistance] → [Physical validation filter] → [TFG body] ↑**********\_\_\_\_**********| (prompt reformulation on detected hallucination)

The methodologically decisive element is not the LLM assistance itself, but the **physical validation filter** interposed between any model output and its incorporation into the text: Kirchhoff's laws, Q-V curves, rotor swing equation and primary source cross-checking. When the filter detects an inference incompatible with system mechanics, the prompt is reformulated with additional semantic constraints and the cycle restarts.

## Validation and verification: four cases of erroneous inference

The use of generative models in a domain as causally dense as power system dynamics reveals, systematically, a behaviour that electrical systems do not tolerate: **inference by statistical analogy**. LLMs tend to apply _typical_ causal patterns — the most frequent in their training corpus literature — to cases whose physical structure is _atypical_. The 28 April event is, due to its dual nature (voltage stability rather than frequency balance), atypical relative to the majority of blackouts documented in 20th-century technical literature, making the observation of where the AI «defaulted» away from the actual phenomenon especially productive.

<ForensicTable 
    title="TABLA 15 | LLM HEURISTIC FAILURE MODES"
    source="Elaboración propia"
  >

| Phenomenon | LLM default erroneous inference | Physical correction applied | Corrective prompt strategy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **UFLS paradox** | Underfrequency load shedding «saved» areas of the system by restoring active power balance. | UFLS is voltage-blind: by disconnecting load it removed inductive reactive power sinks during a capacitive transient, aggravating the overvoltage. | Explicit restriction: reason exclusively in the Q-V plane, ignoring the frequency–active power logic habitual in classic blackouts. |
| **Tap-Lag** | OLTCs responded correctly to the transient, proportionally raising or lowering secondary voltage. | The intentional OLTC time delays — designed to prevent _hunting_ — left them out of phase with a millisecond-scale transient, multiplying voltage towards the 220 kV and 132 kV networks. | Injection of the actual OLTC electromechanical time constants and prohibition of assuming quasi-instantaneous tap changer response. |
| **Meshing capacitive injection** | The meshing manoeuvre reduced system impedance and therefore increased voltage stability. | Under low-load conditions, meshing activated the shunt admittance of the 400 kV lines (Ferranti Effect), injecting the 1,050 MVAr capacitive power that precipitated the overvoltage. | Restriction to «unloaded line» regime and requirement to calculate the reactive power balance with the capacitive admittance $Y_t$ in the line π model. |
| **0.6 Hz oscillation** | Production of an _integrated_ response — the «most probable» reading averaged across sources. | The mode origin (forced oscillation from a specific plant per ICAI; natural system mode aggravated by operational state per REE) is precisely the discrepancy the TFG must preserve, not editorially resolve. | Veto on unilateral choice between the two hypotheses and obligation to produce dual versions with explicit source attribution. |



</ForensicTable>

### The UFLS paradox case

The most illustrative case of the error pattern: when queried about load shedding's role in the incident, models systematically produced an interpretation inherited from classic blackouts, where UFLS constitutes the last line of defence and typically preserves portions of the grid by recovering the frequency–active power balance. This inference is physically correct for the universe of events on which the model was trained, but invalid for 28 April: in a collapse dominated by the Q-V plane, UFLS activation simultaneously removed the inductive reactive power sinks provided by the disconnected loads, **aggravating the overvoltage instead of mitigating it**.

Correction required formulating the prompt with an explicit restriction on the analysis plane and manually verifying that the resulting reasoning was consistent with the NREL oscillography in the 12:33:19–12:33:27 CEST window.

### The Tap-Lag case

The qualitative description models produce of OLTCs is correct in steady state, but by default assumes a proportional, instantaneous response that the actual electromechanical assembly does not possess. The intentional delay introduced to prevent _hunting_ translated on 28 April into a transformation ratio out of phase with the electrical transient, multiplying the overvoltage towards the 220 kV and 132 kV networks — a phenomenon invisible to the operator's SCADA, anchored to 400 kV primary measurements. The entire Tap-Lag causal chain required pre-loading the model with the OLTC time constants and prohibiting it from assuming quasi-instantaneous response.

### The meshing capacitive injection case

The estimated injection of 1,050 MVAr capacitive had to correspond to the effect of the shunt admittance ($Y_t$) of the 400 kV lines operating in no-load conditions (Ferranti Effect). Validation consisted of reproducing the reactive power balance on the line π model, cross-checking the order of magnitude against oscillography and the IIT-ICAI report's independent diagnosis.

### The 0.6 Hz oscillation case

This case illustrates a specific limitation of AI use in forensic contexts with institutional divergence. Models tend to produce an integrated response — the «most probable» reading averaged across sources — when forensic rigour requires preserving the divergence. The mode origin is precisely the datum the TFG must present as an unresolved discrepancy, not as an editorial consensus.

The general observation these four cases support: **the utility of automated assistance is maximal in _processing_ tasks** — extraction, synthesis, structuring, tabulation, assisted writing — **and minimal, to the point of being counterproductive, in _causal inference_ tasks** about physical phenomena with low representation in training corpora.

## Critical reflection: AI in engineering research

The documented experience leads to a structural conclusion, neither triumphalist nor catastrophist: generative models are powerful _accelerators_ of the researcher's cognitive processes, but operate on a probabilistic logic that does not coincide with the deterministic logic governing the physics of material systems.

### Methodological implication

AI use **does not exempt the researcher from mastering the technical content** of their subject; on the contrary, it demands it with greater severity. Only a researcher with sufficient technical competence to identify a physically impossible inference can safely employ a model capable of producing it with rhetorical fluency. The asymmetry between the linguistic plausibility of the output and its material correctness constitutes the primary risk associated with using these tools in demanding technical domains, and can only be neutralised through content mastery that the tool cannot provide.

### Ethical-academic implication

Automated assistance was employed in this work as a processing tool, not as a substitute for reasoning. Every content decision — problem framing, source hierarchy, causal thesis formulation on the 28 April collapse, comparative assessment of institutional narratives, final conclusions — is the author's exclusive responsibility. **AI does not sign theses or sit before examination boards**: the engineer signs their name to the material causality of the facts presented, and that signature is non-transferable.

### Prospective disciplinary implication

The power systems of the coming decade — dominated by power electronics, with dynamics relevant at the sub-cyclic scale and with voltage-reactive interactions that conventional operators cannot capture in real time — will require decision support tools combining the processing speed of algorithmic models with the physical robustness of PSS/E-type simulators. The integration is non-trivial: simulators solve equations; LLMs approximate probability distributions.

The hybrid architecture **— LLMs as semantic interface and synthesis engine, physical simulators as causal inference engine —** is plausibly the direction towards which power systems engineering tools will evolve. Its development will require exactly the same epistemological vigilance that structured this TFG's workflow: always maintaining clarity about what each tool does and what it is explicitly asked not to do.

The detailed record of the restrictive prompt flows employed, together with representative examples of the corrections applied, is documented in the AI Methodology Annex, following the emerging best practice recommendations for transparent integration of generative models in undergraduate and postgraduate research.

<GlitchTitle>2026 Update: One Year Later</GlitchTitle>

The blackout of April 28, 2025 marked a systemic turning point. As of May 2026, the final reports from <GlossaryLink term="ENTSO-E">ENTSO-E</GlossaryLink> (published on March 20, 2026) and independent forensic investigations have brought to light a series of technical and regulatory revelations that drastically alter the initial narrative of the incident.

## 1. The "Overvoltage-Driven Blackout" Paradigm

Initial analyses suggested a classic collapse due to lack of inertia or frequency deviation. However, the independent study by the Institute for Research in Technology (IIT) at Universidad Pontificia Comillas —peer-reviewed in *ScienceDirect* (Rouco, Lobato, Echavarren, 2026)— has introduced an unprecedented technical concept: the **overvoltage-driven blackout**.

:::warning [Technical Revelation]
The fatal sequence was not a generalized voltage drop. Upon activation of the protection logics, the grid suffered a cascade of massive overvoltage trips. The load shedding and the enormous injection of capacitive energy from the 400 kV lines (without sufficient connected reactors) raised voltages above the generation protection limits. The trip of the 400/220 kV transformer in Granada at 12:32:57, which lost 355 MW, was the trigger for the cascade.
:::

According to the forensic reconstruction, the plants connected via <GlossaryLink term="Grid-Following (GFL)">Grid-Following</GlossaryLink> inverters operating in **fixed power factor** mode reacted to active power oscillations by injecting enormous reactive power ramps. In a weakened grid (with a low <GlossaryLink term="Short-Circuit Ratio (SCR)">Short-Circuit Ratio</GlossaryLink>), the <GlossaryLink term="Phase-Locked Loop (PLL)">PLL</GlossaryLink> of these inverters caused instabilities that the system was unable to dampen.

## 2. Operational Opacity and the Role of HVDC

One of the most controversial points of the investigation has been the actions of the system operator (<GlossaryLink term="Red Eléctrica de España (REE)">REE</GlossaryLink>). In July 2025, the independent consortium (AELEC, INESC TEC, Compass Lexecon) denounced a severe lack of transparency regarding the data from state estimators and Phasor Measurement Units (<GlossaryLink term="PMU">PMU</GlossaryLink>). 

The most critical finding of the investigation commissions reveals that, just minutes before the blackout, REE modified the operating mode of the INELFE <GlossaryLink term="HVDC">HVDC</GlossaryLink> link between Spain and France. The link went from its "AC emulation" mode to constant DC power control, neutralizing its ability to dampen the lethal 0.6 Hz oscillation.

## 3. Institutional Consequences and Multimillion-Dollar Litigation

The blackout not only broke the electrical system, but also the institutional relations of the sector, sparking an unprecedented judicial avalanche:

- **CNMC Proceedings**: Since April 2025, 66 disciplinary proceedings have been initiated. REE and Almaraz face "very serious" charges (up to €60M). Concurrently, eleven generation companies (including Endesa, Iberdrola, and Mercuria Solar) face "serious" charges for non-compliance with grid codes.
- **Massive Civil Lawsuits**: Upon expiration of the statute of limitations in April 2026, industrial giants like **Repsol** have formally filed lawsuits against the system for **125 million euros** in lost profits and damages to petrochemical complexes. Iryo and Moeve have also notified their intention to sue.
- **Classified Audios**: The hearings of the Senate Investigation Commission have made public audios from the REE control room. In them, the operators attributed the severe oscillations and voltage instabilities at 12:00 to *"the poor management of a high-power photovoltaic plant in Badajoz"*, revealing that the risk was imminent minutes before the final collapse.

## 4. The Regulatory Response: The Grid-Forming Mandate

Faced with the evidence of structural failure, <GlossaryLink term="ENTSO-E">ENTSO-E</GlossaryLink> published its awaited "Phase II Report" in November 2025, laying the foundations for the new European grid code (NC RfG 2.0).

:::info [The New GFM Standard]
The regulatory draft mandates <GlossaryLink term="Grid-Forming (GFM)">Grid-Forming</GlossaryLink> technology for all new non-synchronous plants and storage systems larger than **1 MW**. It requires a current response time of < 10 ms, ride-through against phase angle jumps, and the provision of synthetic inertia equivalent to that of a synchronous machine.
:::

Despite the Iberian collapse, the official adoption of NC RfG 2.0 by the European Commission has been deprioritized until late 2026. However, countries like the UK (*Stability Pathfinder* project) and Spain have accelerated on their own.

### The Iberian Storage Boom
The systemic cost of keeping the system reinforced with gas after the blackout amounted to an additional **666 million euros** in just ten months. As a direct reaction, the Spanish battery market experienced an "electroshock": the installed BESS (Battery Energy Storage Systems) capacity has **multiplied by 589%**, going from a symbolic 28 MW to almost 200 MW operational in a single year, driving a native grid architecture for <GlossaryLink term="Black Start">Black Start</GlossaryLink> services.

## Conclusion of the Crisis

In retrospect, the "2025 blackout" is no longer studied in 2026 as a fortuitous accident derived from the hydraulic drought or the solar surplus. It is the first documented exponent of a collapse caused by regulatory strangulation and a technological transition that removed synchronous machines before deploying their electronic equivalents. The Iberian Peninsula became by force the living laboratory that has forced Europe to rewrite the rules of electrical stability for the next decade.
