<GlitchTitle>Conclusions</GlitchTitle>

This chapter closes the forensic analysis by articulating two complementary planes: a comparative synthesis of institutional positions and the structural implications that the episode projects onto supply security in the context of the European energy transition. Both share a methodological premise sustained throughout the work: 28 April 2025 is not a frequency incident, but a **voltage collapse in the Q-V plane**, and that distinction is the axis on which the entire subsequent argumentative architecture pivots.

## Comparative synthesis of institutional positions

The reconstruction of 28 April 2025 has produced four families of technically autonomous narratives, each anchored in a distinct analytical framework and responsibility perimeter:

<ForensicTable 
    title="TABLA 17 | ENERGY TRANSITION STRUCTURAL TRILEMMA"
    source="Elaboración propia"
  >

| Agent | Analytical framework | Root cause | Inertia ($H$)† | Prioritised measures |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Government (CSN Committee / REE)** | Regulatory compliance and national security; multifactorial analysis centred on generation fleet response. | Voltage instability precipitated by a systemic deficit in inductive <GlossaryLink term="Potencia reactiva">reactive power</GlossaryLink> absorption; partial P.O. 7.4 non-compliance by the generation fleet. | 2.3 s (peninsular average) | P.O. 7.4 update (BOE-A-2025-13076); reinforced operating regime through 2030; progressive deployment of BESS with <GlossaryLink term="GFM (Grid-Forming)">Grid-Forming</GlossaryLink> capability. |
| **Generator sector (IIT-ICAI / AELEC / Compass Lexecon)** | Electromagnetic transient analysis; expert critique of system operation. | Capacitive instability induced by the <GlossaryLink term="Mallado">meshing</GlossaryLink> manoeuvre under conditions of low synchronous strength, aggravated by observability limitations on the 220 kV network (<GlossaryLink term="Tap-Lag">Tap-Lag</GlossaryLink>). | 1.3 s (South) / 1.84 s (Centre) | Revision of meshing operational protocols; 220 kV observability reinforcement; selective deployment of <GlossaryLink term="Compensadores Síncronos (SynCons)">synchronous condensers</GlossaryLink> at critical nodes. |
| **European system manager (<GlossaryLink term="ENTSO-E">ENTSO-E</GlossaryLink>)** | Continental synchronous area stability; critique of the <GlossaryLink term="Criterio N-1">*N*−1 Criterion</GlossaryLink> against ultra-fast dynamic phenomena. | Propagation of <GlossaryLink term="Oscilaciones electromecánicas">inter-area oscillations</GlossaryLink> and loss of synchronism at the Pyrenean border; exhaustion of the <GlossaryLink term="EAS (ENTSO-E Awareness System)">EAS</GlossaryLink> static tools for anticipating the transient. | Zonal values compatible with IIT-ICAI analysis. | <GlossaryLink term="NC RfG">NC RfG</GlossaryLink> 2.0 with mandatory _Grid-Forming_ capability for PPMs types B–D (≥ 1 MW); reform of EAS operational states. |
| **Independent academic analysis (NREL / MIT CEEPR / Brattle)** | Reconstruction based on <GlossaryLink term="PMU (Phasor Measurement Unit)">PMU</GlossaryLink> records and stability analysis in <GlossaryLink term="IBR">IBR</GlossaryLink>-dominated systems. | Convergence with the capacitive thesis; emphasis on nodal strength (SCR) erosion and mass IBR disconnection through overvoltage protection. | 1.3–1.8 s (southern peninsula) | Ancillary service market redesign towards <GlossaryLink term="Servicios Esenciales de Confiabilidad (ERS)">ERS</GlossaryLink> remunerating inertia, FFR, dynamic reactive power and short-circuit power. |



</ForensicTable>

_† The inertia value discrepancy is not a minor methodological divergence: the global 2.3 s value corresponds to the peninsular average, while the zonal 1.3 s values (southern area) reflect the inertia available at the geographical epicentre of the meshing manoeuvres and the initial disconnection cascade. The 28 April event was not a failure of the average, but a failure of the **weakest zone under local stress** — a circumstance that a global indicator cannot capture by construction._

:::note Robust technical consensus across all four agents Three convergence points emerge from the contrast between the four narratives that **no expert report contradicts**:

**First**, the dominant collapse mechanism was not a frequency loss from inertia deficit, but a <GlossaryLink term="Estabilidad de tensión">voltage instability</GlossaryLink> in capacitive regime precipitated by the combination of minimum residual synchronous generation and underloaded 400 kV lines during the demand valley.

**Second**, prolonged operation under «light grid» conditions, with 82% instantaneous non-synchronous penetration, had structurally exhausted dynamic voltage control margins in the preceding weeks, as evidenced by the precursor events of 22 and 24 April.

**Third**, the regulatory framework in force on 28 April — P.O. 7.4 with asymmetric dead band, NC RfG without _Grid-Forming_ requirements — was structurally inadequate for mobilising damping resources within the timescale the transient required.
:::

The divergences organise the institutional disagreement across two clear axes.

**The measurement perimeter axis.** The CSN Committee and REE compute inertia as a global peninsular metric (2.3 s), while IIT-ICAI and NREL reports work with disaggregated zonal values (1.3 s in the southern area). Both values are arithmetically correct and substantively different: 28 April was not a failure of the average, but of the weakest zone under local stress.

**The trigger attribution axis.** The CSN Committee and REE focus on insufficient reactive power absorption by the generation fleet — an omission by the party obligated under P.O. 7.4. IIT-ICAI focuses on the System Operator's meshing manoeuvre and the structural observability limitation on the 220 kV network through _Tap-Lag_ — an operational decision and an instrumental limitation. Both diagnoses are compatible with the oscillographic evidence: the capacitive transient exceeding 2.4 GVAr simultaneously required a decision that triggered it and an inability to respond that prevented its containment. The disagreement is **not technical but distributive**: it concerns the attribution of responsibility within a causal chain that all reports recognise.

Read together, the four narratives do not constitute mutually exclusive interpretations of the same fact, but **partial projections of a multi-layer phenomenon** onto each agent's respective analytical framework and institutional responsibility perimeter. Interpretive divergence is not noise to be resolved in favour of one position: it is forensic data in itself, revealing how the dynamic complexity of modern power systems exceeds any individual agent's capacity to produce an exhaustive reconstruction of the incident.

## Structural implications: the energy transition trilemma

The 28 April collapse cannot be read as a random accident, but as the empirical manifestation of a set of structural tensions that the European energy transition leaves unresolved. Decarbonisation is not the cause of the collapse: it is the boundary condition that, without being accompanied by a symmetric adaptation in the technical, regulatory and economic planes, converted latent vulnerability into incident.

The Iberian power system operates under a **structural trilemma** in which each edge represents a concrete operational tension between two vertices:

| Tension | Conflicting vertices | Concrete 28 April manifestation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Synchronous displacement / low network strength** | Decarbonisation ↔ Dynamic stability | Merit order displaced CCGTs, draining the system of inertia and short-circuit power at the critical moment. |
| **Merit order / zero or negative price hours** | Decarbonisation ↔ Affordability | Over 500 zero or negative price hours in 2024; daily average price of €18.50/MWh on 28 April itself. |
| **Cost of Essential Reliability Services (ERS)** | Dynamic stability ↔ Affordability | Ancillary services for inertia, dynamic reactive power and FFR were not explicitly remunerated in the market design. |

_28 April 2025 represents the episode in which the three tensions converged without the prevailing regulatory and market framework being able to arbitrate between them._

### Technological tension

The gap between the actual generation fleet and the fleet the system needs to operate safely under IBR-dominated conditions. The replacement of large synchronous alternators by <GlossaryLink term="GFL (Grid-Following)">grid-following</GlossaryLink> inverters has deprived the network of two services that rotating machines provided without explicit remuneration: genuine <GlossaryLink term="Inercia (H)">rotational inertia</GlossaryLink> and the short-circuit power needed to sustain the SCR at transmission network nodes. The technical exit architecture — convergent across expert reports — combines distributed deployment of BESS with Grid-Forming capability for sub-cyclic voltage management with selective installation of synchronous condensers, including the <GlossaryLink term="Estrategia Brownfield">Brownfield</GlossaryLink> reconversion of decommissioned fossil plant alternators.

### Regulatory tension

The inadequacy of the inherited operating framework for governing a fast- dynamic network. The P.O. 7.4 update via the CNMC Resolution of 12 June 2025 — with explicit dynamic requirements and the first-ever inclusion of IBR and storage in the voltage control service — constitutes a step in the correct direction. However, the October 2025 rejection of raising the compliance threshold from 75% to 90% evidences the temporal asymmetry between new asset capabilities and those of the synchronous fleet they replace. At the European level, consolidation of Grid-Forming requirements in ENTSO-E's Phase II Technical Report (November 2025) and its projection onto the future NC RfG 2.0 configure the technical framework of the post-carbon grid — though the current deprioritisation of the European Commission adoption schedule creates an uncertainty window that national operators are managing through transitional measures outside the network code.

### Economic tension

The tension that expert reports identify as the ultimate constraint on the viability of the technical redesign. The pure marginalist energy model is structurally incapable of remunerating the systemic attributes that underpin stability: inertia, short-circuit power, dynamic reactive power and <GlossaryLink term="Fast Frequency Response (FFR)">Fast Frequency Response</GlossaryLink>. The proliferation of zero or negative price hours — over **500 hours in 2024**, with a daily average price of **€18.50/MWh** on 28 April itself — is not a defect of renewable design, but the signal that stability attributes are absent from the market's objective function. The transformation of these services into explicit commercial products under the category of Essential Reliability Services (ERS) constitutes the economic prerequisite without which the preceding technical and regulatory framework lacks medium-term sustainability.

At the European governance scale, the episode revealed the limitations of the EAS in fulfilling its declared early warning function. The Iberian system transitioned from «Normal» to «Blackout» state without passing through any of the intermediate states prescribed by the <GlossaryLink term="SO GL (System Operation Guidelines)">System Operation Guidelines</GlossaryLink>. The implication is structural: security tools built on static load flow analyses and the *N*−1 Criterion are inadequate for networks with high power electronics penetration, whose relevant dynamics occur on sub-second timescales. The pan-European coordination architecture requires incorporating dynamic nodal strength indicators, zonal inertia indices and grid-forming capacity metrics as standardised state parameters exchangeable between Transmission System Operators.

## The lesson of 28 April

The structural lesson of 28 April, taken in its entirety, is not that the energy transition is too ambitious or that decarbonisation compromises supply security. The lesson is that the transition, to be operationally sustainable, **must occur simultaneously across the three planes the trilemma identifies**: technical, regulatory and economic. Any asymmetry between them — a transformed generation fleet with an inherited network code; an updated network code without a market to remunerate the services it requires; a redesigned market without the physical assets capable of providing them — reproduces the vulnerability conditions that 28 April materialised.

The analytical value of this work resides, ultimately, in having shown that the four institutional narratives **coexist without cancelling each other** and that none of them, taken alone, exhausts understanding of the incident. Forensic synthesis requires treating expert reports not as rival hypotheses about the same fact, but as partial projections of a complex phenomenon onto each agent's respective framework. Only triangulated reading — which preserves divergences rather than dissolving them — allows the extraction of the structural conditions that converted a routine deep-decarbonisation operating scenario into the first systemic _blackout_ of the continental synchronous area in two decades.

Those conditions, far from being extraordinary, are present in every European power system in transition: **28 April 2025 is, in this sense, less an Iberian accident than a European precedent**.

<GlitchTitle>Summary of Figures</GlitchTitle>

## The largest blackout in the continental European system in over 20 years

April 28, 2025, will be recorded as the date the Iberian peninsula experienced an unprecedented total electrical collapse in modern European history. In just 32 seconds —between 12:32:57 and 12:33:29 CEST— a cascade of generation disconnections engulfed peninsular Spain and continental Portugal in a blackout that interrupted the supply of demand on the order of 25.2 GW to approximately 57 million people.

What follows is a numerical summary of the incident through six interactive visualizations that document the magnitude of the event, its technical causes, the mechanism of its development, and the exceptional operational response that allowed recovery in approximately 18.5 hours.

---

### 1. The immediate impact: Six figures that define a crisis

<Bloque1KPI />

The collapse was so rapid and total that most regional operators had no time to implement corrective maneuvers. The first generation trips —occurring between seconds 0 and 20 of the cascade— eliminated approximately 2,500 MW of generation capacity from a peninsular grid operating with a demand in the range of 29.6 GW.

But these figures, although enormous, hide a more subtle reality: the blackout was not caused by a lack of available energy (the system had sufficient generation), but by a catastrophic failure in voltage control of a grid where the vast majority of generation was operated by power electronics without dynamic stabilization capacity (the 82% detailed in §2.3).

---

### 2. Generation at the time of collapse: An unbalanced system

<Bloque2MixGeneracion />

At 12:30 CEST, moments before the collapse, the Spanish peninsular system operated with a total generation on the order of 29.6 GW. The composition of that generation revealed an extreme concentration in technologies based on electronic converters, particularly in solar photovoltaic energy (see [**Table 15**](./15-galeria-de-tablas.mdx) in the Table Gallery for the exact metric breakdown by technology).

This distribution is the structural context of the incident. Synchronous generation —that is, rotating machines (nuclear, hydro, gas turbines) that produce alternating current by electromagnetic rotation— represented only 18% of the instantaneous mix. The remaining 82% operated through electronic power inverters (mostly Solar PV + Wind) configured at that time for reactive power control in "fixed power factor" mode, without dynamic voltage adjustment capability.

This imbalance is fundamental to understanding why the blackout occurred. In a traditional 20th-century grid, dominated by synchronous generation, a sudden loss of approximately 2,500 MW would have caused a severe but controllable frequency drop through the rotational inertia of the generators (typically H > 3 seconds). In the Iberian peninsula on April 28, the equivalent inertia of the system was only in the range of 2.3 seconds, barely sufficient for regulatory margins, and the response to the disturbance depended entirely on the ability of the inverters to sustain voltage and phase angle. When that capability collapsed, the system collapsed with it.

---

### 3. The 32-second cascade: Chronology of the collapse

<Bloque3Cascada />

The incident unfolded in a strictly chronological sequence that crossed the point of no return at 24 seconds. The detailed progression of the loss of load, from the root trip in Granada to the final zero voltage (including the frequency nadir at 47.79 Hz), is consolidated in the interactive [**Timeline (Table 16)**](./16-galeria-forense.mdx).

---

### 4. The frequency drop: The window of instability

<Bloque4Frecuencia />

System frequency is the vital pulse of an electrical grid. In normal operation, it maintains a stable value of 50 Hz (in continental Europe). Every 0.1 Hz deviation triggers low or high-level protections, because a frequency deviation indicates an imbalance between demand and generation.

During the 27 seconds of the collapse, the frequency behaved like an electrocardiogram of a dying system:

- **Seconds −2 to 0**: Stable at 50.00 Hz. Normal system.
- **Seconds 0–19**: Slow drop to 49.95 Hz. The system absorbs the first trip (Granada, −355 MW) without immediate alarm.
- **Second 19.34 onwards**: Accelerated drop. At 21 seconds: 49.30 Hz. Pumping UFLS protections are activated (49.5 Hz, then 49.3 Hz).
- **Second 22**: 49.00 Hz. Activation of industrial transport load UFLS. The system attempts load shedding (reduce demand) but the rate of change of frequency (ROCOF) is higher than what protections can handle.
- **Second 23.53**: 48.46 Hz. AC trip France. Import is lost. ROCOF remains ≤ 1 Hz/s, but the margin is zero.
- **Second 24**: 47.79 Hz (nadir). Activation of nuclear plants and HVDC blocking.
- **Second 24.5 onwards**: Collapse. Zero voltage. Undefined frequency.

The maximum recorded ROCOF (Rate of Change of Frequency) was approximately 1.0–1.2 Hz/s in 100-millisecond windows during the cascade, exceeding at several moments the dynamic margins that inverters can follow. This is the physical essence of the incident: a grid with 82% electronic generation facing a disturbance that unfolded faster than that generation could respond to.

---

### 5. Interconnections: The geographical factor that confined the crisis

<Bloque5Interconexiones />

One of the structural factors of the collapse was the low interconnection of the Iberian peninsula with the rest of the continental European system at 12:30 CEST (the meticulous breakdown of physical flows, exports, and saturation degrees of each cross-border link is detailed in [**Table 14**](./15-galeria-de-tablas.mdx) and [**Forensic Charts 1-5**](./16-galeria-forense.mdx)).

The interconnection ratio —the quotient between import capacity and total demand— was approximately 3–5%. This means that, even in the best scenario, peninsular Spain had an external support capacity of only in the range of 900 MW to 1,500 MW for a system with a typical demand of 25–30 GW. That is, approximately 3–5 minutes of coverage in case of loss of internal generation.

During the cascade (12:33:19), when the system attempted to import massively from France to sustain voltage, the inverters requested transient flows of up to 4,609 MVAr (reactive power), which exceeded the safe operation limits of the AC interconnection, whose nominal active power capacity is 2,700 MW (equivalent thermal limit on the order of 3,000 MVA in apparent power). This accelerated the propagation of instability towards France, activating ENTSO-E border isolation protections (AC lines trip at 48.46 Hz, 12:33:21.535).

Unlike Italy (2003) or France (2006), where greater interconnection allowed a quick distribution of the recovery effort, the Iberian peninsula remained confined and isolated, forcing an autonomous restoration from zero.

---

### 6. Restoration: approximately 18.5 hours from electrical zero

<Bloque6Cronologia />

Barely 2 minutes after electrical zero (12:35 CEST), Red Eléctrica Española requested EDP Portugal to independently start the Castelo do Bode hydroelectric plant (138 MW, Zêzere basin). This action was the first step of what would become one of the most complex restoration operations ever recorded in Europe.

The chronology was as follows:

**12:43–12:44 CEST (Duration: 10–11 minutes from zero)**
Re-energization of the first transmission artery: the Hernani substation in the Basque Country receives supply from the interconnection with France. Initial import: on the order of 31 MW (barely 0.1% of pre-blackout demand).

**12:45 CEST (WEST: 11:45, _Western European Summer Time_ used in Portugal)**
Castelo do Bode (Portugal) successfully connects to the REN 220 kV busbar. Autonomous start in approximately 10 minutes. First Portuguese electrical island created. REN operators begin gradual expansion towards Lisbon and the Tagus.

**13:35 CEST**
Synchronization of the Baixàs–Vic line (France–Catalonia, 400 kV east). Second artery from France. Expansion towards the Mediterranean coast.

**18:36 CEST (WEST: 17:36)**
Aldeadávila–Pocinho synchronization (220 kV): First Spain–Portugal high voltage interconnection. Portugal connects to the continental European frequency. Spanish black-start schemes (BS-Duero 1, BS-Extremadura, BS-Aragón) activated in chain since approximately 16:00 CEST.

**23:00 CEST (Duration: approximately 10.5 hours from zero)**
Recovery: 51% of peninsular demand (12,847 MW active). 70% of transmission substations energized. Hospitals, essential services, and most distribution networks restored. Still around 8% of the population without supply, mainly in isolated rural areas.

**00:22 CEST – April 29**
Portuguese transmission grid 100% restored (total duration for Portugal: approximately 12 hours).

**04:00 CEST – April 29**
Spanish transmission grid 100% restored. Accumulated time from zero: approximately 15.5 hours. Distribution in the last mile restoration process.

**07:00 CEST – April 29 (Total duration: approximately 18.5 hours)**
99.95% of peninsular demand recovered. Barely small isolated rural areas still without coverage. Completely stable system. Normal voltage and frequency. Operational end of the incident.

**Autonomous start (black-start) plants were the bottleneck and the critical factor in the restoration:**

- **Castelo do Bode (Portugal, EDP)**: Hydroelectric, 138 MW. Started in approximately 10 minutes thanks to water stored in the Zêzere basin. Cost of black-start service: in the range of 240,000 €/year (Portuguese Government announced extension to 2030 and incorporation of Alqueva and Baixo Sabor on April 29).
- **Aldeadávila (Spain, Iberdrola)**: Reversible hydroelectric in the Duero, approximately 1,100 MW (pump + turbine). BS-Duero scheme activated around 16:00 CEST. Controlled start capacity without external support guaranteed by stored water and gradual synchronization capability.

The Iberian system, in retrospect, was saved by the luck that two strategically located hydroelectric plants had autonomous start capacity. Without Castelo do Bode and Aldeadávila, restoration would have required sustained import from France, an issue that would have complicated operational coordination with RTE and ENTSO-E for additional critical hours.

---

## Conclusion: From figures to structure

The six preceding visualizations are not mere numbers. They are the translation of a profound systemic failure: a modern network, decarbonized, efficient in production, but fatally unbalanced in its generation composition, controlled by protection systems designed for a 20th-century paradigm that no longer existed.

The blackout of April 28, 2025, was inevitable given the parameters of that day. But it was avoidable with long-term policies: greater synchronous inertia, better interconnection, mandatory dynamic control in renewables, and —more fundamentally— an energy transition speed that respected the limits of inertia and stability of the grid.

The lesson, recorded in 27 seconds of cascade and approximately 18.5 hours of restoration, has reshaped the European electrical architecture. April 28, 2025, was the day the continental electrical engineering had to admit that the 20th century had ended and the future required new laws, not just new machines.

# Introduction

## Object and Scope

The primary object of this Final Degree Project (TFG) consists of critical and comparative study of technical, regulatory, and operational narratives formulated by various electrical sector actors, based on information and reports published in response to the **Voltage Zero** (_blackout_) event that occurred in the Iberian synchronous system on April 28, 2025.

This event involved sudden loss of more than **15 GW of generation** in mere seconds and left approximately **60 million people** without electrical supply, constituting one of the episodes of systemic instability of greatest magnitude recorded in continental Europe in recent decades.

The exceptional nature of the collapse—characterized by cascade of disconnections associated with overvoltage phenomena in context of high penetration of <GlossaryLink term="IBR">_Inverter-Based Resources_ (IBR</GlossaryLink>)—generated profound interpretive disagreement regarding its root causes and assignment of technical and operational responsibilities.

### Three Institutional Narratives

This investigation focuses on critical examination of divergences and consensus points existing between three predominant institutional visions:

#### Administration Vision (Government and Redeia)

The report of the National Security Council Analysis Committee and the System Operator articulates interpretation grounded in regulatory compliance and technical discipline of generation fleet. According to this perspective, the system possessed sufficient regulatory tools to mitigate the transient, attributing event aggravation to insufficient absorption of <GlossaryLink term="Potencia reactiva">inductive reactive power</GlossaryLink>—a deficit that prevented containing voltage escalation—as established in Operating Procedure **P.O. 7.4**.

#### Generation Sector Vision (ICAI/AELEC Report)

The independent technical report elaborated by IIT-ICAI and Compass Lexecon locates root cause in concrete operational decisions adopted by System Operator. This narrative questions meshing maneuver executed by Redeia, arguing it significantly increased network capacitive contribution in scenario of low <GlossaryLink term="Potencia de cortocircuito">synchronous strength</GlossaryLink>, generating overvoltage pulse aggravated by operator observability limitations over 220 kV network (<GlossaryLink term="Tap-Lag">Tap-Lag phenomenon</GlossaryLink>).

#### European Manager Vision (ENTSO-E)

The factual report published by ENTSO-E introduces perspective oriented to continental synchronous area stability, analyzing propagation of inter-area oscillations and indicating limitations of traditional static security approaches based on _N-1 Criterion_ against ultrafast dynamic phenomena characteristic of systems with high power-electronics-based generation penetration.

![Replication of collapse sequence](/figuras/albustami_ieee39_secuencia.png)

The scope of this TFG is circumscribed to technical scrutiny of these argumentative frameworks through their contrast with European network codes (_Network Codes_, especially RfG Regulation) and with modern principles of stability in electrical systems dominated by inverters.

---

## Technical Justification: Iberian System Vulnerability

Transition toward decarbonized generation model has structurally transformed peninsular system dynamics. Accelerated replacement of conventional synchronous plants by Inverter-Based Resources reduces rotating masses coupled to network and, with them, both system <GlossaryLink term="Inercia (H)">**inertia** ($H$</GlossaryLink>)—which fell to zonal values between 1.3 s and 1.8 s in peninsular south, below 2 s threshold that technical literature associates with compromised dynamic margins—and available **short-circuit power** at nodes.

This dual reduction does not affect only frequency–active power axis: it weakens also, and critically, system capacity to dynamically absorb reactive power ($Q$) and sustain voltage against fast transients, which is precisely the axis on which April 28 collapse was articulated.

This structural vulnerability manifested extremely on April 28, 2025. Morning of incident, system operated with **82% non-synchronous renewable penetration**, in context of _valley demand_ that reduced load in transport corridors and exacerbated <GlossaryLink term="Efecto Ferranti">capacitive effect</GlossaryLink> of 400 kV lines. To balance generation, operator decoupled practically entire available thermal units, leaving synchronous generators at historical minimums.

![Electromechanical metamorphosis of power system](/figuras/futured_grid_evolution.png)

Operating under "light grid" paradigm contracts stability margins nonlinearly. Unlike synchronous alternators, IBR fleet operates practically entirely in <GlossaryLink term="GFL (Grid-Following)">grid-following</GlossaryLink> mode: their inverters need stable external voltage ($V$) and frequency ($f$) as synchronism reference. With synchronous units drastically reduced, system lost its principal mechanism of dynamic reactive power absorption, eliminating natural damping against voltage transients.

To this internal fragility adds structural condition of Iberian Peninsula as **"energy island"**: its interconnection capacity with France sits far below community directives, preventing import of dynamic stability from continental core. Convergence of both factors—low synchronous strength and relative network isolation—configured vulnerability making impossible to brake overvoltage cascade.

![Electrical interconnection level versus peak demand](/figuras/mit_interconnection_stats.png)

---

## Research Methodology

This investigation's methodology is based on **comparative forensic analysis** oriented to reconstruct April 28, 2025 event sequence through triangulation of divergent primary sources. The process was articulated in three methodological phases:

1. **Primary source compilation**: Systematic study of official technical reports, which are themselves sustained in processing of over 170 GB of technical records by System Operator, including SCADA telemetry and oscillographic records.

2. **Narrative triangulation**: Systematic contrast of Administration thesis versus generation sector technical analysis regarding meshing management and 220 kV network inobservability.

3. **Cross-technical validation**: Collation of chronological sequences from each report with independent inter-area oscillation analysis published by NREL based on <GlossaryLink term="PMU (Phasor Measurement Unit)">Phasor Measurement Unit (PMU</GlossaryLink>) data, whose continental coverage permits arbitration between divergent versions.

![Topological location of Phasor Measurement Units (PMUs) in Europe](/figuras/pmu_sensors_europe.png)

Given volume of technical documentation generated after incident, large-scale language models were employed as documentary assistance tool. Their application focused on report classification and synthesis, extraction of critical data, and identification of recurrent failure patterns between different sources.

Nevertheless, use of these tools was strictly circumscribed to documentary organization and synthesis. Language models present known limitations against fast-dynamics phenomena—such as interpretation of <GlossaryLink term="UFLS (Underfrequency Load Shedding)">UFLS paradox</GlossaryLink> or Tap-Lag mechanism—so technical comparison, causality assessment, and work conclusions are exclusive responsibility of author's judgment.

## Historical and Forensic Context

Forensic and economic indicators derived from the expert analysis and audit reports of the April 28 incident.

<div style={{ display: 'grid', gridTemplateColumns: 'repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr))', gap: '1.25rem', margin: '2rem 0' }}>
  <Link to="/datos-tiempo-real/costes-ajuste" style={{ textDecoration: 'none', color: 'inherit' }}>
    <div className="card-hover-effect" style={{ border: '1px solid var(--ifm-color-emphasis-200)', borderRadius: '12px', padding: '1.5rem', height: '100%', display: 'flex', flexDirection: 'column', justifyContent: 'space-between' }}>

import GlossaryLink from '@site/src/components/GlossaryLink';

# El impacto en Francia y Portugal

The 28 April Iberian voltage collapse did not stop at the Pyrenees or the Guadiana. The violence of the electrodynamic transient radiated a shockwave through the interconnections, subjecting the French network to extreme operational stress and dragging the Portuguese system into a total blackout from which it could only emerge through seventeen hours of ground-up restoration. These two episodes — one contained, one catastrophic — precisely illustrate the conditions that determine whether a system can reject a perturbation of this magnitude or succumb to it.

## France (RTE): the system that held at the limit

### The Golfech 1 trip and negative sequence currents

The propagation mechanism towards France was dominated by a sudden, massive excess of capacitive <GlossaryLink term="Potencia reactiva">reactive power</GlossaryLink>. Seconds before separation, the <GlossaryLink term="HVDC">HVDC</GlossaryLink> Baixas–Santa Llogaia link was absorbing **870 MVAr**, acting as a dynamic reactive power sink at the border. The instantaneous loss of this sink, combined with the opening of 400 kV lines that remained energised no-load from the French side — generating reactive power through the capacitive <GlossaryLink term="Efecto Ferranti">Ferranti Effect</GlossaryLink> — induced a severe transient overvoltage profile that propagated rapidly across the entire southwest of France.

Facing this voltage escalation, RTE's secondary voltage control forced the large synchronous alternators in the region to operate deep into their underexcitation capability curves. The most critical case was **Golfech Nuclear Unit 1**, a **1,290 MW** generating block. To contain the voltage profile, its Automatic Voltage Regulators (AVR) drastically reduced rotor excitation current, driving the machine to absorb **426 MVAr** at 12:33 CEST.

This extreme operating condition severely compromises machine stability. As the air-gap magnetic flux decreases, the synchronising torque maintaining the rotor coupled to the network frequency weakens. Simultaneously, the asymmetric character of the border opening transients generated significant negative sequence currents in the 400 kV network. Symmetrical components theory establishes that negative sequence currents produce a magnetic field rotating in the opposite direction to the rotor at synchronous speed, inducing double-frequency (100 Hz) eddy currents in the solid rotor body and retaining rings, causing adiabatic heating within seconds.

At **12:33:35.759 CEST** — just **fifteen seconds** after the Iberian collapse — the combination of underexcitation instability and phase imbalance heating irremediably activated the generator's internal protection relays (loss-of-excitation relay ANSI 40 and negative sequence / current imbalance relay ANSI 46), forcing the trip and total disconnection of Golfech

1. The simultaneous loss of the HVDC link and this nuclear pillar obliged RTE to reconfigure its load flows from more northerly regions to avoid a cascading collapse of its own. The reactor was successfully resynchronised to the network on 29 April.

### Subtransmission network trip: the Dax–Arriosses 63 kV line

The impact was not limited to conventional generation. The most revealing record of the violence of the electrodynamic transient in France was the trip of the **63 kV overhead line Dax–Arriosses** at **12:33:20.551 CEST**, ordered by its loss-of-synchronism protections (ANSI 78 relay), configured to act on the first beat of the oscillation.

The actuation of a loss-of-synchronism protection at the 63 kV level is extraordinarily anomalous: power swinging is normally detected on 400 kV corridors. Its appearance at 63 kV indicates that the <GlossaryLink term="Phase-Locked Loop (PLL)">PLLs</GlossaryLink> of a massive inverter aggregation in Aquitaine lost their angular reference relative to the main network due to the asymmetric transient and overvoltage. The relay interpreted the cyclical current reversal of the uncontrolled inverters as a classic rotating machine loss of synchronism, isolating the sub-network.

| Critical element in France | Time (CEST) | Technical cause | Systemic impact |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HVDC Baixas–Santa Llogaia | 12:33:20 | Loss of Iberian receiving network | Sudden loss of 870 MVAr sink |
| 63 kV line Dax–Arriosses | 12:33:20.551 | Loss-of-synchronism relay (1st beat) | Sub-network isolation and local IBR disconnection |
| Nuclear Unit Golfech 1 (1,290 MW) | 12:33:35.759 | Underexcitation limit / ANSI 40 and 46 relays | Loss of 426 MVAr absorption; structural thermal stress |

### RTE as «infinite bus» during Top-Down restoration

At **12:40 CEST**, the voltage profile in southwest France stabilised. From that moment, the RTE network assumed an irreplaceable structural role: providing a firm electromagnetic anchor for the Spanish system's restoration via a Top-Down strategy.

In power systems theory, an **«infinite bus»** is an idealised voltage source with infinite inertia and zero Thévenin equivalent impedance. In practice, with France solidly connected to the immense inertial mass of Continental Europe, its 400 kV network behaved operationally as an infinite bus for the collapsed Iberian network.

At **12:39 CEST**, REE formally requested RTE to restore voltage at Hernani substation from the French Argia substation. At **12:41 CEST**, RTE agreed to channel up to **400 MW initially** to stabilise the first reconnections in northern Spain. By closing the border circuit breaker, France imposed its nominal frequency (50.00 Hz) and rigid voltage control on the first Spanish node. This imported short-circuit power absorbed the brutal reactive imbalances and active load steps inevitably produced when energising no-load 400 kV lines. Without the inertial anchor of this French infinite bus, REE's restoration attempts would have been subject to unbearable oscillations that would have retripped their protections. Throughout the afternoon, this stabilising French flow increased to **1,400 MW**, constituting the backbone of Spanish system normalisation.

## Portugal (REN): the dragged collapse and Bottom-Up restoration

### Why Portugal could not isolate

While France had a rigid network capable of rejecting the perturbation by cutting its links, REN operated with such dense electrical and geographical coupling with Spain that configuring an isolated island operation in time was physically impossible. Portugal succumbed to a dragged collapse dominated by reactive-voltage (Q-V) coupling: trips in southern Spain withdrew critical reactive absorption nodes, the overvoltage propagated without resistance to Portuguese substations, and the frequency decline activated the combined <GlossaryLink term="UFLS (Underfrequency Load Shedding)">UFLS</GlossaryLink> schemes of REE and REN. Despite massive load shedding, the <GlossaryLink term="RoCoF (Rate of Change of Frequency)">RoCoF</GlossaryLink> was so extreme that circuit breaker mechanical delays (50–100 ms) made it impossible to balance the system before minimum-frequency protections tripped the last thermal turbines.

| Frequency threshold (Hz) | Load shed — Portugal (MW) | Load shed — Spain (MW) | Total (MW) |
| :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: |
| 49.0 | 381 | 1,669 | 2,050 |
| 48.8 | 450 | 1,575 | 2,025 |
| 48.6 | 438 | 1,524 | 1,962 |
| 48.4 | 218 | 1,294 | 1,512 |
| 48.2 | 470 | 2,168 | 2,638 |
| 48.0 | 359 | 588 | 947 |

_Combined REE and REN UFLS actuation by frequency threshold. Source: REN and REE PMU records._

### Restoration: a chronicle of failures and solutions

With no external links available, REN executed a pure <GlossaryLink term="Black Start">Bottom-Up</GlossaryLink> restoration based entirely on its own autonomous start-up resources. The sequence exposes the severe limitations that the laws of electromagnetism impose on this process.

**12:35–12:45 CEST — First island at Zêzere.** REN ordered the autonomous black start of HPP 1-Centro. By 12:45, the plant was operating in isochronous mode, successfully energising the 220 kV busbar at Zêzere substation.

**12:49 CEST — Collapse from sympathetic inrush.** The restoration protocol required energising Transformer 4 at Zêzere (170 MVA, 220/60 kV). On closing the 220 kV circuit breaker, HPP 1-Centro tripped instantly. The cause was the **sympathetic inrush current phenomenon**: a 170 MVA transformer, when energised from a weak network — a single hydroelectric unit with low short-circuit power and high subtransient impedance — demands a magnetising current that can exceed nominal current by an order of magnitude, characterised by high second-harmonic content and extremely low power factor. The isolated generator could not supply this reactive power surge; the transient voltage collapse activated the protection relays. Subsequent attempts to start auxiliary generators within the plant failed repeatedly over the next three hours.

**12:43–16:38 CEST — Combined-cycle control system failures.** At 12:43, REN dispatched the black start order for CCGT 1-Norte. Despite the gas turbine responding mechanically, the plant was unable to close the generator circuit breaker for hours: the substation's DC battery banks had discharged during the prolonged blackout, leaving the high-voltage circuit breaker closing coils without power. The blockage was resolved at **16:38 CEST**.

**15:40–15:55 CEST — Second attempt and renewed collapse.** After reconfiguration work, HPP 1-Centro restarted at 15:40 and energised the Zêzere 220 kV busbar. At 15:51, a local demand block of **5 MW** was connected, but the island's inertial fragility was such that load fluctuations triggered another trip at 15:55.

### The decisive manoeuvre: Torrão as a pure synchronous condenser

It was evident that the island lacked the necessary stiffness (short-circuit power) to absorb load steps. After restarting HPP 1-Centro at **16:13 CEST**, REN executed at **17:23 CEST** a technically sophisticated manoeuvre: it started **HPP Torrão Unit 2**, not to inject active power, but in **pure <GlossaryLink term="Compensadores Síncronos (SynCons)">synchronous condenser</GlossaryLink> mode**.

Operating a hydroelectric plant as a synchronous condenser involves emptying the turbine chamber by injecting pressurised air (_runner dewatering_), allowing the runner to spin freely in air while coupled to the network. The generator consumes a marginal amount of active power to overcome mechanical bearing friction, but through excitation control instantaneously injects or absorbs massive quantities of <GlossaryLink term="Potencia reactiva">reactive power</GlossaryLink>. Critically, Torrão's enormous rotating mass contributed pure kinetic <GlossaryLink term="Inercia (H)">inertia</GlossaryLink> and multiplied the short-circuit power of the Zêzere island.

This manoeuvre acted as an electrodynamic damper. Island voltage stabilised, enabling from **16:26 CEST** progressive load restoration on the 60 kV and 150 kV networks and voltage extension to HPP 2 and HPP 3 Centro. At **16:38 CEST**, the second secure restoration zone was established from CCGT 1-Norte.

### 0 MW synchronisation and full normalisation

By 20:00 CEST, the two Portuguese islands had been internally meshed but were still operating asynchronously relative to Spain and the rest of Europe. The most delicate step was coupling with the REE network, already synchronised with the French infinite bus.

At **20:25 CEST**, the interconnection was closed under one non-negotiable technical requirement: a **0 MW exchange programme**. The underlying physics is governed by the inter-area active power transfer equation:

$$P = \frac{V_1 V_2}{X} \sin\delta$$

To close the interconnection breaker without generating a destructive synchronising power surge, the phase angle difference ($\delta$) between the Portuguese and Spanish nodes had to be exactly zero, with equal voltage magnitudes. By setting a 0 MW setpoint in the Automatic Generation Control (AGC) systems, operators ensured neither network would attempt to export inertia to the other at the coupling instant. An error would have forced a violent power flow, tripping the directional protections and plunging Portugal into a second blackout.

With the manoeuvre successful, Portugal recovered its continental synchronous reference. The robustness provided by the interconnection allowed acceleration of remaining demand restoration, achieving full normalisation at **00:22 on 29 April** — **seventeen hours** after the voltage zero.

title: "El impacto en Francia y Portugal"

import GlossaryLink from '@site/src/components/GlossaryLink';
import GlitchTitle from "@site/src/components/GlitchTitle";

<GlitchTitle>El impacto en Francia y Portugal</GlitchTitle>

El colapso del sistema eléctrico ibérico no se detuvo en los Pirineos ni en el Guadiana. La violencia del transitorio electrodinámico del 28-A irradió una onda de choque a través de las interconexiones que sometió a la red francesa a un estrés operativo extremo y arrastró al sistema portugués a un apagón total del que solo pudo salir mediante una restauración de diecisiete horas desde cero. Estos dos episodios —uno contenido, el otro catastrófico— ilustran con precisión las condiciones que determinan si un sistema puede rechazar una perturbación de esta magnitud o sucumbir ante ella.

## Francia (RTE): el sistema que resistió en el límite

### El disparo de Golfech 1 y las corrientes de secuencia negativa

El mecanismo de propagación hacia Francia estuvo dominado por un exceso súbito y masivo de <GlossaryLink term="Potencia reactiva">potencia reactiva</GlossaryLink> capacitiva. Segundos antes de la separación, el enlace <GlossaryLink term="HVDC">HVDC</GlossaryLink> Baixas–Santa Llogaia absorbía **870 MVAr** actuando como sumidero dinámico de regulación de tensión en la frontera. La pérdida instantánea de este sumidero, combinada con la apertura de las líneas de 400 kV que quedaron energizadas en vacío desde el lado francés —generando reactiva por <GlossaryLink term="Efecto Ferranti">efecto Ferranti</GlossaryLink> capacitivo—, indujo un perfil de sobretensiones transitorias severas que se propagó velozmente por todo el suroeste francés.

Frente a esta escalada, el control secundario de tensión de RTE forzó a los grandes alternadores síncronos de la región a operar en subexcitación profunda. El caso más crítico fue la **Unidad 1 de la central nuclear de Golfech**, un bloque de **1.290 MW** de potencia nominal. Para contener el perfil de tensiones, sus reguladores automáticos de tensión (AVR) redujeron drásticamente la corriente de excitación del rotor, llevando a la máquina a absorber la cifra de **426 MVAr** a las 12:33 CEST.

Esta condición extrema compromete severamente la estabilidad de la máquina. Al reducirse el flujo magnético en el entrehierro, el par sincronizante que mantiene al rotor acoplado a la frecuencia de la red se debilita. Simultáneamente, el carácter asimétrico de los transitorios de apertura en la frontera generó corrientes de secuencia negativa considerables en la red de 400 kV. La teoría de componentes simétricas establece que estas corrientes producen un campo magnético giratorio en sentido opuesto al giro del rotor, induciendo corrientes parásitas de doble frecuencia (100 Hz) en el cuerpo macizo del rotor y en los anillos de retención, con calentamiento adiabático severo en cuestión de segundos.

A las **12:33:35.759 CEST** — apenas **quince segundos** después del colapso ibérico — la combinación de inestabilidad por subexcitación y calentamiento por desbalance de fases activó los relés de protección interna del generador (relé de pérdida de excitación ANSI 40 y relé de desbalance / corriente de secuencia negativa ANSI 46), forzando el disparo y la desconexión total de Golfech 1. La pérdida simultánea del HVDC y de este pilar nuclear obligó a RTE a reconfigurar sus flujos desde regiones más septentrionales para evitar un colapso en cascada propio. El reactor fue resincronizado satisfactoriamente a la red el 29 de abril.

### Disparo en la red de subtransmisión: la línea Dax-Arriosses (63 kV)

El impacto no se limitó a la generación convencional. El registro más revelador de la violencia del transitorio en Francia fue el disparo de la **línea aérea de 63 kV Dax–Arriosses** a las **12:33:20.551 CEST**, ordenado por las protecciones de pérdida de sincronismo (relé ANSI 78), configuradas para actuar en el primer latido (_first beat_) de la oscilación.

La actuación de una protección de pérdida de sincronismo en un nivel de 63 kV es extraordinariamente anómala: las oscilaciones de potencia (_power swinging_) suelen detectarse en corredores de 400 kV. Su aparición en 63 kV indica que los <GlossaryLink term="Phase-Locked Loop (PLL)">PLL</GlossaryLink> de una agregación masiva de inversores en Aquitania perdieron su referencia angular respecto a la red principal por el transitorio asimétrico y la sobretensión. El relé interpretó la inversión cíclica de las corrientes de los inversores descontrolados como una pérdida de sincronismo clásica de máquinas rotativas, aislando la subred.

| Elemento crítico en Francia | Hora (CEST) | Causa técnica | Impacto sistémico |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Enlace HVDC Baixas–Santa Llogaia | 12:33:20 | Pérdida de la red ibérica receptora | Pérdida súbita de sumidero de 870 MVAr |
| Línea 63 kV Dax–Arriosses | 12:33:20.551 | Relé de pérdida de sincronismo (1er latido) | Aislamiento de subred y desconexión de IBRs locales |
| Unidad Nuclear Golfech 1 (1.290 MW) | 12:33:35.759 | Límite de subexcitación / relés ANSI 40 y 46 | Pérdida de absorción de 426 MVAr; estrés estructural |

### RTE como "nodo infinito" durante la restauración Top-Down

A las **12:40 CEST**, el perfil de tensiones en el suroeste francés logró estabilizarse. A partir de ese instante, la red de RTE asumió un rol estructural insustituible: proporcionar un anclaje electromagnético firme para la restauración del sistema español mediante una estrategia Top-Down.

En la teoría de sistemas de potencia, un **"nodo infinito"** (_infinite bus_) es una fuente de tensión con inercia infinita e impedancia de Thévenin equivalente nula. En la práctica, al estar Francia conectada solidariamente a la inmensa masa inercial de Europa Continental, su red de 400 kV se comportó operativamente como un nodo infinito para la colapsada red ibérica.

A las **12:39 CEST**, REE solicitó formalmente a RTE la reposición de tensión en la subestación de Hernani desde la subestación francesa de Argia. A las **12:41 CEST**, RTE acordó canalizar hasta **400 MW iniciales** para estabilizar las primeras reconexiones en el norte de España. Al cerrar el interruptor fronterizo, Francia impuso su frecuencia nominal (50,00 Hz) y su control de tensión rígido sobre el primer nudo español. Esta potencia de cortocircuito importada absorbió los brutales desequilibrios de reactiva y los escalones de carga activa inevitables al energizar líneas de 400 kV en vacío. Sin el anclaje inercial de este nodo infinito francés, los intentos de REE por restablecer la tensión habrían estado sujetos a oscilaciones insoportables que habrían disparado nuevamente sus protecciones. A lo largo de la tarde, el flujo estabilizador francés se incrementó hasta los **1.400 MW**, constituyendo la columna vertebral de la normalización del sistema español.

## Portugal (REN): el colapso arrastrado y la restauración Bottom-Up

### Por qué Portugal no pudo aislarse

Mientras Francia disponía de una red rígida capaz de rechazar la perturbación cortando los enlaces, la infraestructura de <GlossaryLink term="REE">REN</GlossaryLink> operaba con un acoplamiento eléctrico y geográfico tan denso con España que configurar una operación en isla aislada a tiempo resultó físicamente imposible. Portugal sucumbió en un colapso arrastrado dominado por el acoplamiento reactiva-tensión (Q-V): los disparos en el sur de España retiraron nudos críticos de absorción reactiva, la sobretensión se propagó sin resistencia hacia las subestaciones portuguesas, y el descenso de frecuencia activó los esquemas combinados de <GlossaryLink term="UFLS (Underfrequency Load Shedding)">UFLS</GlossaryLink> de REE y REN. A pesar del deslastre masivo, el <GlossaryLink term="RoCoF (Rate of Change of Frequency)">RoCoF</GlossaryLink> fue tan pronunciado que los retardos mecánicos de los disyuntores (50–100 ms) hicieron imposible equilibrar el sistema antes de que las protecciones de mínima frecuencia desengancharan las últimas turbinas térmicas.

| Umbral de frecuencia (Hz) | Carga deslastrada en Portugal (MW) | Carga deslastrada en España (MW) | Total (MW) |
| :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: |
| 49,0 | 381 | 1.669 | 2.050 |
| 48,8 | 450 | 1.575 | 2.025 |
| 48,6 | 438 | 1.524 | 1.962 |
| 48,4 | 218 | 1.294 | 1.512 |
| 48,2 | 470 | 2.168 | 2.638 |
| 48,0 | 359 | 588 | 947 |

_Actuación combinada del UFLS de REE y REN por escalones de frecuencia. Fuente: registros PMU de REN y REE._

### La restauración: crónica de fallos y soluciones

Sin ningún enlace externo disponible, REN ejecutó una restauración <GlossaryLink term="Black Start">Bottom-Up</GlossaryLink> basada íntegramente en sus propios recursos de arranque autónomo. La secuencia expone las severas limitaciones que las leyes del electromagnetismo imponen al proceso.

**12:35–12:45 CEST — Primera isla en Zêzere.** REN ordenó el arranque autónomo de la HPP 1-Centro. A las 12:45, la central operaba en modo isócrono y logró energizar la barra de 220 kV de la subestación de Zêzere. Se había formado la primera isla.

**12:49 CEST — Colapso por _sympathetic inrush_.** El protocolo exigía energizar el Transformador 4 de Zêzere (170 MVA, relación 220/60 kV). Al cerrar el interruptor, HPP 1-Centro disparó instantáneamente. La causa fue el **fenómeno de _sympathetic inrush current_**: un transformador de 170 MVA, al ser energizado desde una red débil —una única máquina hidroeléctrica con baja potencia de cortocircuito y alta impedancia subtransitoria—, demanda una corriente magnetizante que puede exceder en un orden de magnitud la corriente nominal, con alto contenido de armónicos de segundo orden y factor de potencia extremadamente bajo. El generador aislado no pudo proveer esta ráfaga de potencia reactiva; el hundimiento transitorio de tensión activó los relés de protección. Los intentos de arrancar pequeños grupos auxiliares dentro de la misma planta fracasaron durante las siguientes tres horas.

**12:43–16:38 CEST — Fallos en los ciclos combinados.** Paralelamente, REN despachó a las 12:43 la orden de arranque autónomo para el CCGT 1-Norte. A pesar de que la turbina de gas respondió mecánicamente, la central fue incapaz de cerrar el interruptor del generador durante horas: los bancos de baterías de corriente continua de la subestación presentaban caída de tensión por descarga prolongada, dejando sin alimentación las bobinas de cierre de los disyuntores de alta tensión. El bloqueo se solventó finalmente a las **16:38 CEST**.

**15:40–15:55 CEST — Segundo intento y nuevo colapso.** Tras labores de reconfiguración, HPP 1-Centro reinició a las 15:40 y logró energizar nuevamente la barra de 220 kV. A las 15:51 se conectó un bloque de demanda local de **5 MW**, pero la fragilidad inercial de la isla fue tal que las fluctuaciones provocaron un nuevo disparo a las 15:55.

### La maniobra decisiva: Torrão como compensador síncrono puro

Era evidente que la isla carecía de la rigidez necesaria (potencia de cortocircuito) para absorber escalones de carga. Tras reiniciar HPP 1-Centro a las **16:13 CEST**, REN ejecutó a las **17:23 CEST** una maniobra de máxima sofisticación técnica: arrancó la **Unidad 2 del HPP Torrão**, pero no para inyectar potencia activa, sino en **modo de <GlossaryLink term="Compensadores Síncronos (SynCons)">compensador síncrono</GlossaryLink> puro**.

Operar una central hidroeléctrica como compensador síncrono implica vaciar la cámara de la turbina inyectando aire a presión (_depresión de la cola de agua_), permitiendo que el rodete gire libremente en el aire acoplado a la red. El generador consume una cantidad marginal de potencia activa para vencer la fricción mecánica, pero mediante el control de su sistema de excitación inyecta o absorbe masivas cantidades de <GlossaryLink term="Potencia reactiva">potencia reactiva</GlossaryLink> de manera instantánea. Más crítico aún: la enorme masa rotante del rotor de Torrão aportó <GlossaryLink term="Inercia (H)">inercia</GlossaryLink> cinemática pura y multiplicó la potencia de cortocircuito de la isla de Zêzere.

Esta maniobra actuó como amortiguador electrodinámico. La tensión en la isla se estabilizó, permitiendo desde las **16:26 CEST** la reposición progresiva de carga en las redes de 60 kV y 150 kV y la extensión de tensión a las plantas HPP 2 y HPP 3 Centro. A las **16:38 CEST** se estableció la segunda zona segura de restauración desde el CCGT 1-Norte.

### Sincronización a 0 MW y normalización total

Hacia las 20:00 CEST, las dos islas portuguesas habían sido malladas internamente, pero seguían operando de manera asíncrona respecto a España y el resto de Europa. El paso más delicado era el acoplamiento con la red de REE, ya sincronizada con el nodo infinito francés.

A las **20:25 CEST**, se procedió al cierre de la interconexión bajo un requisito técnico innegociable: un **programa de intercambio de 0 MW**. La física subyacente se rige por la ecuación de transferencia de potencia entre dos áreas síncronas:

$$P = \frac{V_1 V_2}{X} \sin\delta$$

Para cerrar el interruptor de interconexión sin generar un transitorio destructivo de potencia sincronizante, la diferencia de ángulo de fase ($\delta$) entre el nodo portugués y el español debía ser exactamente cero y las magnitudes de tensión iguales. Al establecer una consigna de 0 MW en los sistemas de Control Automático de Generación (AGC), los operadores garantizaron que ninguna de las dos redes intentara exportar inercia hacia la otra en el instante del acoplamiento. Un error habría forzado un flujo violento, disparando las protecciones direccionales y precipitando a Portugal en un segundo apagón.

Con el éxito de la maniobra, Portugal recuperó la referencia síncrona continental. La robustez proporcionada por la interconexión permitió acelerar el levantamiento del resto de la demanda, alcanzando la normalización total a las **00:22 del 29 de abril** — **diecisiete horas** después del cero de tensión.

# Coordinación Continental

The abrupt separation of the Iberian Peninsula from the Continental European synchronous system was not merely an infrastructure incident: it was the first real-conditions test of the pan-European power grid governance architecture designed following the great European blackout of 2006. This chapter documents how that institutional architecture responded — its speed, its successes and its limitations — from the first seconds of the collapse to the final resynchronisation.

## Synchronous Area Monitors (SAM): activation of unified command

<GlossaryLink term="ENTSO-E">ENTSO-E</GlossaryLink>'s governance architecture designates **Synchronous Area Monitors** (SAM) to assume macroscopic coordination control in events threatening the integrity of Continental Europe. In April 2025, these roles fell to **Swissgrid** (Switzerland) and **Amprion** (Germany). The 28 April contingencies in Spain, Portugal and France fell directly under Swissgrid's supervisory domain.

The <GlossaryLink term="EAS (ENTSO-E Awareness System)">ENTSO-E Awareness System (EAS)</GlossaryLink> — an encrypted, centralised communications platform — operated as the nervous system of crisis management. The dispatch timeline reveals the speed at which a supranational unified command was structured:

| Time (CEST) | Sender | Recipient | Message / Strategic decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 12:34–12:36 | REE | REN | Mutual confirmation of total blackout; agreement to set exchange programmes at 0 MW. |
| 12:39 | Amprion | Swissgrid | Formal _System Split_ alert confirmation on EAS portal, activating the European emergency state. |
| 12:41 | Swissgrid | RTE | Status update request; RTE confirms plans to send 400 MW initial support to REE. |
| 12:47 | REE | Swissgrid | Official _Blackout_ report from Madrid; sharing of initial Top-Down restoration schemes. |
| 12:47 | TERNA | RTE | Italian TSO offers active support and flow flexibility on the eastern French border. |
| 12:49–12:54 | Swissgrid / Amprion | All (CE) | Formalisation of unified command structure. |
| 15:50 | Amprion | RTE | Alert over anomalous PICASSO requests of 2,500 MW associated with negative prices. |

The critical window is **12:49 to 12:54 CEST**: in just five minutes, the SAMs applied ENTSO-E's standardised system separation protocol, assigning three differentiated roles with exclusive, non-overlapping authority:

**<GlossaryLink term="REE">REE</GlossaryLink> — Iberian Frequency Leader.** Exclusive mandate to balance the generation/demand ratio within the isolated bloc, managing load shedding and gradual start-up without external interference.

**Swissgrid — Continental European Frequency Leader.** Control of the remainder of the synchronous area, orchestrating Frequency Containment Reserves (FCR) across more than 20 countries to compensate for the sudden over-frequency generated by the loss of exports to the peninsula and the HVDC Baixas shutdown.

**RTE — Resynchronisation Leader.** Absolute authority over closing operations on the transpyrenean links. Neither REE nor any other entity could operate a border circuit breaker without prior validation of the slip and voltage parameters from RTE's control rooms in Paris and Toulouse.

## The role of Coreso: the mathematical shield of restoration

While national TSOs operated physical circuit breakers, the Regional Coordination Centre (RCC) **Coreso** (Brussels) executed an immense computational task to ensure that crisis solutions did not trigger new blackouts.

As the afternoon progressed, emergency power transfers from France to Spain escalated, with transient imports negotiated up to **2,000 MW**. These massive injections severely modify the natural load flows across French, Swiss and German networks. Coreso, using **Coordinated Security Analysis** (CSA) tools, processed AC load flows on the **unified European model** (CGM) in near-real time.

Its objective was to verify strict compliance with the <GlossaryLink term="Criterio N-1">*N*−1 Criterion</GlossaryLink>: to certify through simulation that if, while France was exporting 2,000 MW of support, an internal French or German corridor was suddenly lost, the remaining interconnected network would not suffer thermal overloads or voltage range violations. Simultaneously, the Nordic RCC led the **Short-Term Adequacy** (STA) analysis, confirming to the SAMs that rolling capacity was available in central Europe to sustain this effort without jeopardising the evening demand peak in donor countries.

Coreso's validation was the **mathematical shield** that allowed RTE to operate with tactical confidence. Without it, the risk of instability propagating from the peninsula towards the continental network core would have forced severe limits on support flows, slowing recovery considerably.

## The limitations the EAS could not conceal

Multinational coordination functioned with notable effectiveness once the emergency state was activated. However, the episode starkly exposed the structural limitations of the European monitoring system in the preceding phase: as documented in the analysis of the Spanish system, the Iberian bloc transitioned directly from «Normal» to «Blackout» state (criterion OB3) without passing through any of the intermediate Alert or Emergency states prescribed by the <GlossaryLink term="SO GL (System Operation Guidelines)">System Operation Guidelines</GlossaryLink>.

As a result, neighbouring operators — RTE, Swissgrid, Coreso — received no anticipatory signals of dynamic vulnerability south of the Pyrenees. The first activation of the SAM/EAS architecture was not preventive but reactive: the EAS acted as a post-mortem notifier of the collapse, not as an early warning tool. This limitation — the European monitoring system's inability to capture fast voltage dynamics in low-inertia networks — is one of the incident's central regulatory lessons and the starting point for the reforms documented in the following section.

Communication was maintained continuously until the end of the emergency, culminating at **00:11 CEST on 29 April**, when RTE notified Swissgrid that REE's Automatic Generation Control (AGC) algorithm was once again in a stabilised closed loop — the signal certifying the end of the continental emergency state.

<GlitchTitle>Coordinación Continental</GlitchTitle>

La separación abrupta de la península ibérica del sistema síncrono de Europa Continental no fue solo un incidente de infraestructura: fue el primer test en condiciones reales del sistema de gobernanza paneuropea de redes eléctricas diseñado tras el gran apagón europeo de 2006. Este capítulo documenta cómo respondió esa arquitectura institucional — sus velocidades, sus aciertos y sus límites — desde los primeros segundos del colapso hasta la resincronización final.

## Los Monitores del Área Síncrona (SAM): activación del mando unificado

La arquitectura de gobernanza de <GlossaryLink term="ENTSO-E">ENTSO-E</GlossaryLink> designa a los **Monitores del Área Síncrona** (SAM, _Synchronous Area Monitors_) para asumir el control de coordinación macroscópica en eventos que amenazan la integridad de Europa Continental. En abril de 2025, estos roles recayeron sobre **Swissgrid** (Suiza) y **Amprion** (Alemania). Las contingencias del 28-A en España, Portugal y Francia recaían directamente sobre el dominio de supervisión de Swissgrid.

El <GlossaryLink term="EAS (ENTSO-E Awareness System)">ENTSO-E Awareness System (EAS)</GlossaryLink> — una plataforma de comunicaciones encriptada y centralizada — operó como el sistema nervioso de la gestión de la crisis. La cronología de los despachos revela la velocidad a la que se estructuró un mando unificado supranacional:

| Hora (CEST) | Emisor | Receptor | Mensaje / Decisión estratégica |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 12:34–12:36 | REE | REN | Confirmación mutua de apagón total; acuerdo para fijar programas de intercambio en 0 MW. |
| 12:39 | Amprion | Swissgrid | Confirmación de la alerta formal de _System Split_ en el portal EAS, activando el estado de emergencia europeo. |
| 12:41 | Swissgrid | RTE | Petición de actualización; RTE confirma planes para enviar 400 MW de soporte inicial a REE. |
| 12:47 | REE | Swissgrid | Reporte oficial de _Blackout_ desde Madrid; compartición de los primeros esquemas de restauración Top-Down. |
| 12:47 | TERNA | RTE | El TSO italiano ofrece soporte activo y flexibilidad de flujos en la frontera oriental francesa. |
| 12:49–12:54 | Swissgrid / Amprion | Todos (CE) | Formalización de la estructura de mando unificada. |
| 15:50 | Amprion | RTE | Alerta sobre peticiones anómalas de 2.500 MW en PICASSO asociadas a precios negativos. |

La ventana crítica se sitúa entre las **12:49 y las 12:54 CEST**: en apenas cinco minutos, los SAM aplicaron el protocolo estandarizado de separación de sistemas de ENTSO-E, asignando tres roles diferenciados con autoridad exclusiva y no solapable:

**<GlossaryLink term="REE">REE</GlossaryLink> — Líder de Frecuencia Ibérico.** Mandato exclusivo de equilibrar la ratio generación/demanda dentro del bloque aislado, gestionando el deslastre y el arranque paulatino sin interferencias externas.

**Swissgrid — Líder de Frecuencia de Europa Continental.** Control del resto del área síncrona, orquestando las reservas de contención de frecuencia (FCR) en más de 20 países para compensar la súbita sobrefrecuencia generada por la pérdida de las exportaciones hacia la península y el apagado del HVDC Baixas.

**RTE — Líder de Resincronización.** Autoridad absoluta sobre las operaciones de cierre en los enlaces transpirenaicos. Ni REE ni ninguna otra entidad podía operar un interruptor fronterizo sin la validación previa de los parámetros de deslizamiento y tensión desde las salas de control de RTE en París y Toulouse.

## El papel de Coreso: el escudo matemático de la restauración

Mientras los TSOs nacionales maniobran interruptores físicos, el Centro de Coordinación Regional (RCC) **Coreso** (Bruselas) ejecutaba una inmensa labor computacional para garantizar que las soluciones de la crisis no provocaran nuevos apagones.

Al avanzar la tarde, los envíos de potencia de emergencia desde Francia hacia España escalaron hasta negociarse importaciones transitorias de hasta **2.000 MW**. Estas inyecciones masivas modifican severamente los flujos de carga naturales a lo largo de las redes francesas, suizas y alemanas. Coreso, utilizando herramientas de **Análisis de Seguridad Coordinada** (CSA), procesó flujos de carga de corriente alterna sobre el **modelo unificado europeo** (CGM) casi en tiempo real.

Su objetivo era verificar la estricta observancia del <GlossaryLink term="Criterio N-1">Criterio *N*−1</GlossaryLink>: certificar mediante simulaciones que, si mientras Francia exportaba esos 2.000 MW de soporte se perdía súbitamente un corredor interno francés o alemán, la red interconectada restante no sufriría sobrecargas térmicas ni salidas de rango de tensión. Simultáneamente, el Nordic RCC lideró el **Análisis de Adecuación a Corto Plazo** (STA), confirmando a los SAM que existía capacidad rodante disponible en el centro de Europa para sostener este esfuerzo sin poner en riesgo la punta de demanda nocturna de los países donantes.

Esta validación de Coreso fue el **escudo matemático** que permitió a RTE operar con confianza táctica. Sin ella, el riesgo de propagación de la inestabilidad desde la península hacia el núcleo de la red continental habría obligado a limitar severamente el soporte, ralentizando la recuperación.

## Las limitaciones que el EAS no pudo ocultar

La coordinación multinacional funcionó con notable eficacia una vez activado el estado de emergencia. Sin embargo, el episodio expuso con crudeza las limitaciones estructurales del sistema europeo de monitorización en la fase previa: tal como se documenta en el análisis del sistema español, el bloque ibérico transitó directamente del estado "Normal" al estado "Blackout" (criterio OB3) sin pasar por los estados intermedios de Alerta o Emergencia previstos en las <GlossaryLink term="SO GL (System Operation Guidelines)">System Operation Guidelines</GlossaryLink>.

El resultado fue que los operadores vecinos — RTE, Swissgrid, Coreso — no recibieron señales anticipatorias de vulnerabilidad dinámica al sur de los Pirineos. La primera actuación de la arquitectura SAM/EAS no fue preventiva sino reactiva: el EAS actuó como notificador _post mortem_ del colapso, no como herramienta de alerta temprana. Esta limitación — la incapacidad del sistema europeo de monitorización para capturar la dinámica rápida de tensión en redes de baja inercia — es una de las lecciones regulatorias centrales del incidente y el punto de partida de las reformas documentadas en la sección siguiente.

La comunicación se mantuvo constante hasta el fin de la emergencia, culminando a las **00:11 CEST del 29 de abril**, momento en que RTE notificó a Swissgrid que el algoritmo de Control Automático de Generación (AGC) de REE estaba de nuevo en lazo cerrado estabilizado — señal que certificó el fin del estado de emergencia continental.
